fuentes/relacion-de-marcos-de-niza/titul.texto: Account of the discovery of the seven cities

fuentes/relacion-de-marcos-de-niza/sopor.texto: Account signed and sworn in Mexico on September 2, 1539, before Viceroy Antonio de Mendoza

fuentes/relacion-de-marcos-de-niza/resum.texto: Report on Friar Marcos’s journey to the north of New Spain in 1539. He recounts that he sent Estebanico ahead, that Estebanico was killed in Cíbola, and that he himself saw the city from a hill: “greater than the city of Mexico,” with multistory houses. He takes possession of the land for the king with a cross and returns without entering.

fuentes/relacion-de-marcos-de-niza/por_q.texto: His description of Cíbola set off Coronado’s expedition. When the expedition reached the Zuni village of Hawikuh, the soldiers accused him of lying, and historians still debate whether he actually saw the village or invented part of the journey.

fuentes/relacion-de-la-jornada-de-cibola.texto: Account of the Expedition to Cíbola
Written around 1560–1565; known from a copy of 1596 held at the New York Public Library

Account of Coronado’s expedition (1540–1542), written some twenty years later by one of his soldiers. It describes the Zuni, Hopi and Rio Grande peoples, their multistory houses, kivas and agriculture, the “querechos” and “teyas” who followed the bison on the plains, and Quivira. It recounts in detail the Tiguex War, including the burning of prisoners who had surrendered, and criticizes the errors of the leaders.
It is the most complete source on the expedition and on the peoples of the Southwest at the time of contact. Castañeda wrote to defend those who took part, and he acknowledges their abuses.
Castilian text with English translation in The Coronado Expedition, by George Parker Winship (1896), on Internet Archive

fuentes/relacion-del-hidalgo-de-elvas/ti.texto: True Account of the Labors of Governor Hernando de Soto (Hidalgo de Elvas)

fuentes/relacion-del-hidalgo-de-elvas/re.texto: Account by an anonymous Portuguese who took part in Soto’s expedition (1539–1543). It describes the chiefdoms of the Southeast (Apalache, Cofitachequi, Coosa, Tascalusa, Chicaza), their towns with temples on mounds, the battle of Mabila and Soto’s death. It records without concealment the use of chains on porters, punishments and the setting of dogs on Indigenous people.

fuentes/relacion-del-hidalgo-de-elvas/po.texto: It is one of four accounts of the expedition, along with those of Rodrigo Rangel (in Oviedo), Luis Hernández de Biedma and the Inca Garcilaso, and the one most used by historians. Richard Hakluyt translated it into English in 1609 to promote the colonization of Virginia.

fuentes/relacion-del-hidalgo-de-elvas/le.texto: English translation by Buckingham Smith (New York, 1866), on Internet Archive

fuentes/la-florida-del-inca/soporte.texto: History of Adelantado Hernando de Soto, printed in Lisbon in 1605

fuentes/la-florida-del-inca/resumen.texto: History of Soto’s expedition written by the Inca Garcilaso from the oral testimony of a survivor, Gonzalo Silvestre, and the written accounts of two others. It presents the caciques of Florida with speeches and the virtues of classical heroes, to show that Indians were capable of reason and worthy of being evangelized. It gives higher death tolls than the other chroniclers.

fuentes/la-florida-del-inca/por_que_impo.texto: It is the most literary version of the expedition and the least reliable in its figures, but it preserves data that are not in the other accounts. It shows the view of a Cusco-born mestizo on other American peoples.

fuentes/la-florida-del-inca/leer.0.titul.texto: Madrid edition of 1723, on Internet Archive

fuentes/memorial-de-solis-de-meras/titul.texto: Memorial of Gonzalo Solís de Merás on the Expedition of Pedro Menéndez de Avilés

fuentes/memorial-de-solis-de-meras/resum.texto: Account of Pedro Menéndez de Avilés’s campaigns in Florida, written by his brother-in-law, who accompanied him. It recounts the founding of St. Augustine, the capture of Fort Caroline and the execution of the French at Matanzas, which he justifies on the grounds that they were heretics. It also covers the alliances with the Timucua, Guale and Calusa caciques, including Menéndez’s marriage to the sister of the Calusa cacique.

fuentes/memorial-de-solis-de-meras/por_q.texto: It is the Spanish version of the destruction of French Florida, written by a relative with an interest in Menéndez’s grants. It should be read alongside the accounts of Laudonnière and Le Moyne.

fuentes/memorial-de-solis-de-meras/leer..texto: Volume I of La Florida, su conquista y colonización por Pedro Menéndez de Avilés, by Eugenio Ruidíaz y Caravia (1893), which publishes the memorial, on Internet Archive

fuentes/historia-de-la-nueva-mexico/resu.texto: Epic poem in 34 cantos of hendecasyllables that narrates Oñate’s expedition to New Mexico, from the preparations to the capture of Acoma in 1599, including the speeches of the Acoma leaders and the battle. It glorifies the conquistadors and presents the Acoma defense as treachery.

fuentes/historia-de-la-nueva-mexico/por_.texto: It is considered the first printed epic poem about a territory of present-day United States and is a firsthand account by a participant in the capture of Acoma, written when the author and Oñate were under investigation for their abuses.

fuentes/historia-de-la-nueva-mexico/leer.texto: Reprint by the Museo Nacional de México (1900), on Internet Archive

fuentes/proceso-contra-los-indios-de-aco.texto: Records of the trial held in the village of Santo Domingo in February 1599, in the Archivo General de Indias

Court record of Oñate’s trial of the Acoma taken prisoner after the battle of January 1599, with statements from soldiers and Indigenous people. The sentence condemns men over 25 years old to have one foot cut off and to twenty years of personal servitude, young people and women to twenty years of servitude, and gives the children to friars and settlers to be raised.
It is the central document of the harshest episode in the colonization of New Mexico and one of the bases for the condemnation of Oñate in 1614; the actual extent of the amputations is disputed.

fuentes/memorial-de-benavides/titulo.texto: Memorial of Fray Alonso de Benavides

fuentes/memorial-de-benavides/soporte.texto: Memorial presented to Philip IV in 1630 by the Commissary General of the Indies, Fray Juan de Santander; expanded version for the pope in 1634

fuentes/memorial-de-benavides/resumen.texto: Report on the Franciscan missions of New Mexico that lists the villages, languages, churches and baptized people, and describes the Apaches, Navajos and Jumanos. It claims there were tens of thousands of baptized Indians and recounts the miraculous conversion of the Jumanos, which the 1634 version attributes to the nun María de Ágreda, whom Benavides had met in 1631, appearing before them without leaving Spain.

fuentes/memorial-de-benavides/por_que_im.texto: It is the main description of New Mexico before the 1680 revolt; written to obtain more friars and funds, its conversion figures are considered inflated.

fuentes/memorial-de-benavides/leer.0.tit.texto: Copy of the Madrid edition of 1630, on Internet Archive

fuentes/autos-de-otermin/titulo.texto: Proceedings on the Uprising of the Indians of New Mexico (Otermín’s Proceedings)

fuentes/autos-de-otermin/soporte.texto: Diaries, war councils and testimony from Spanish and Indigenous witnesses, in the Archivo General de la Nación de México; translated into English by Charles Hackett in 1942

fuentes/autos-de-otermin/resumen.texto: Documentation gathered by Governor Otermín on the 1680 revolt and the failed attempt at reconquest in 1681. It includes the diary of the siege of Santa Fe and of the retreat, and statements from captive Pueblo Indians, such as the Keres Pedro Naranjo, who attribute the revolt to Po’pay, to orders to destroy everything Christian, and to the rejection of tribute and punishment.

fuentes/autos-de-otermin/por_que_importa.texto: It is almost everything known about the revolt from the inside, although it comes through interrogations of prisoners; historians compare it with the oral traditions of the Pueblo peoples.

fuentes/relacion-historica-palou/titulo.texto: Historical Account of the Life and Apostolic Labors of the Venerable Father Fray Junípero Serra

fuentes/relacion-historica-palou/resumen.texto: Biography of Junípero Serra written by his disciple, with the history of the founding of the missions of Alta California up to 1784. It presents Serra as a model of holiness and the missions as works of conversion and civilization, and narrates episodes such as the Kumeyaay uprising at San Diego in 1775.

fuentes/relacion-historica-palou/por_que.texto: It was the basis of Serra’s image and of the cause for his beatification; it is a direct source for the early years of the missions, written with an apologetic purpose.

fuentes/relacion-historica-palou/leer.0..texto: Mexico City edition of 1787, on Internet Archive

fuentes/escritos-de-junipero-serra/titul.texto: Letters and Writings of Fray Junípero Serra

fuentes/escritos-de-junipero-serra/escri.texto: Mission San Carlos Borromeo de Carmelo

fuentes/escritos-de-junipero-serra/sopor.texto: Edited with English translation by Antonine Tibesar (1955–1966)

fuentes/escritos-de-junipero-serra/resum.texto: Serra’s correspondence with viceroys, governors and Franciscan superiors, and his 1773 Representación to Viceroy Bucareli. It includes his requests that soldiers not mistreat Indigenous women, his defense of missionary authority over the neophytes, his plea for clemency for the Kumeyaay in 1775, and his justification of whipping as paternal punishment.

fuentes/escritos-de-junipero-serra/por_q.texto: It allows the mission system to be read in the words of its founder, with his intentions and methods, and it sustains both his defenders and his critics.

fuentes/instruccion-de-galvez-1786/titul.texto: Instruction Drawn Up by Royal Order for the Government of the Internal Provinces of New Spain

fuentes/instruccion-de-galvez-1786/resum.texto: Instructions from Viceroy Bernardo de Gálvez for the northern frontier. They order unrelenting war against hostile Apaches and offer peace to those who ask for it, with rations, gifts, alcohol and poor-quality firearms to make them dependent on the Spanish, and encourage wars among enemy peoples.

fuentes/instruccion-de-galvez-1786/por_q.texto: It summarizes the Bourbon frontier policy, which on the Apache frontier relied more on diplomacy, trade and “peace establishments” near the presidios than on missions.

fuentes/bref-recit-cartier/titulo.texto: Brief Account of Jacques Cartier’s Second Voyage

fuentes/bref-recit-cartier/resumen.texto: Account of Cartier’s second voyage up the Saint Lawrence River, to the Iroquoian villages of Stadacona and Hochelaga. It describes their longhouses, crops and customs, the scurvy that killed 25 Frenchmen over the winter and its cure with an infusion from a tree the Indigenous people had shown them, and the seizure of the chief Donnacona.

fuentes/bref-recit-cartier/por_que_impor.texto: Together with the accounts of Cartier’s other voyages, it is the only direct description of the Iroquoians of the Saint Lawrence, who disappeared as a people before 1600, and of the first French contacts in Canada.

fuentes/bref-recit-cartier/leer.0.titulo.texto: Paris reprint (1863) of the 1545 text, on Internet Archive

fuentes/les-voyages-de-champlain/titulo.texto: The Voyages of Samuel de Champlain

fuentes/les-voyages-de-champlain/resumen.texto: Accounts of Champlain’s voyages to the Saint Lawrence, Acadia, Lake Champlain and Huronia, with maps. They describe the Montagnais, Algonquins, Hurons and Iroquois, the fur trade, the founding of Quebec, and the campaigns in which he accompanied his allies, such as the 1609 battle against the Mohawk and the attack on an Iroquois village in 1615.

fuentes/les-voyages-de-champlain/por_que.texto: They are the main source on the beginnings of New France and the Franco-Indigenous alliance, written by its protagonist to win support at court.

fuentes/les-voyages-de-champlain/leer.0..texto: Des Sauvages (1603), facsimile from Canadiana on Internet Archive

fuentes/les-voyages-de-champlain/leer.1..texto: English translation by Annie Nettleton Bourne, edited by Edward Gaylord Bourne, on Internet Archive

fuentes/relaciones-de-los-jesuitas/sopor.texto: Annual reports of the mission superiors, printed in Paris by Sébastien Cramoisy; bilingual edition by Reuben Gold Thwaites in 73 volumes (1896–1901)

fuentes/relaciones-de-los-jesuitas/resum.texto: Annual reports of Jesuit missionaries in New France, written by Le Jeune, Brébeuf, Jérôme Lalemant, Ragueneau and others. They describe in detail the languages, religion, economy and politics of the Innu, Hurons, Iroquois and Great Lakes peoples, the epidemics of 1634–1640, the torture and ritual cannibalism of prisoners, the destruction of Huronia and the deaths of the missionaries.

fuentes/relaciones-de-los-jesuitas/por_q.texto: They are the largest written source on the peoples of the Northeast in the 17th century; they were published to attract donors in France, which shaped what they say about conversions.

fuentes/relaciones-de-los-jesuitas/leer..texto: One volume of Reuben Gold Thwaites’s bilingual edition (Cleveland, 1896–1901), on Internet Archive

fuentes/grand-voyage-sagard/titulo.texto: The Great Voyage to the Huron Country

fuentes/grand-voyage-sagard/resumen.texto: Account of the Recollect Sagard’s stay among the Hurons in 1623–1624, with chapters on their villages, agriculture, marriage, medicine, war and treatment of prisoners, and a dictionary of the Huron language. It criticizes French merchants and defends his order’s mission against the Jesuits.

fuentes/grand-voyage-sagard/por_que_impo.texto: Together with Champlain’s accounts, it is one of the earliest and most detailed descriptions of the Hurons before the epidemics of the 1630s.

fuentes/cartas-de-marie-de-l-incarnation.texto: Published by her son, the Benedictine Claude Martin, in 1681

Correspondence of the founder of the Ursulines of Quebec with her son and other religious in France. It recounts life in the convent and the school, its Huron, Algonquin and Iroquois pupils, the Iroquois wars, the epidemics, the 1663 earthquake and the colony’s politics.
It is one of the few women’s testimonies from New France; it reveals the limits of the project to “Frenchify” Indigenous girls, which she herself acknowledges.

fuentes/gran-paz-de-montreal-tratado/tit.texto: Treaty of the Great Peace of Montreal

fuentes/gran-paz-de-montreal-tratado/aut.texto: Louis-Hector de Callière and the chiefs of about forty nations

fuentes/gran-paz-de-montreal-tratado/res.texto: Peace agreement signed on August 4, 1701 by Governor Callière and the representatives of about forty Indigenous nations, who signed with drawings of their clans. The nations commit to peace among themselves, to returning prisoners, and to submitting their disputes to the governor; the Iroquois accept neutrality between the French and the English.

fuentes/gran-paz-de-montreal-tratado/por.texto: It ended almost a century of wars in the Northeast and is one of the great treaties between Europeans and Indigenous peoples in the Americas; the original is held in French archives.

fuentes/ordenanza-de-raudot-1709/titulo.texto: Ordinance of Intendant Raudot on the Panis and Black Slaves

fuentes/ordenanza-de-raudot-1709/resumen.texto: Ordinance of April 13, 1709 by the intendant of New France declaring that the Indians called Panis and the Black people bought or to be bought belong in full ownership to those who purchased them as slaves, and punishing anyone who helps them escape.

fuentes/ordenanza-de-raudot-1709/por_que.texto: It gave legal basis to the enslavement of Indigenous people and Africans in New France, which already existed in practice; the Panis captives came from wars among peoples of the West and were bought from the French allies.

fuentes/histoire-de-la-louisiane/resumen.texto: History and description of French Louisiana in three volumes. It devotes much attention to the Natchez, among whom the author lived: their chief the Great Sun, the division between nobles and “stinkards,” the temple of the fire and the 1725 funerals of the war chief Tattooed Serpent, in which wives and servants were strangled; it also narrates the 1729 rebellion.

fuentes/histoire-de-la-louisiane/por_que.texto: It is the main description of the Natchez, the last chiefdom of the Mississippian tradition seen by Europeans; written thirty years later, it mixes observation and reconstruction.

fuentes/histoire-de-la-louisiane/leer.0..texto: Volume I of the Paris edition of 1758, on Internet Archive

fuentes/histoire-de-la-louisiane/leer.1..texto: English translation of 1774 on Project Gutenberg

fuentes/histoire-de-la-nouvelle-france-c.texto: History and General Description of New France

History of New France from Cartier to 1736, written by a Jesuit who taught in Quebec and traveled the Great Lakes and the Mississippi in 1720–1722; it includes the diary of that journey in the form of letters. It describes Indigenous peoples sympathetically and with the idea that the French treated them better than the English and the Spanish did.
For a century it was the standard history of New France and a source widely used by Enlightenment writers.
Volume I of the Paris edition of 1744, on Internet Archive

fuentes/histoire-notable-de-la-floride/r.texto: Account of the Huguenot colonies of Charlesfort (1562) and Fort Caroline (1564–1565), written by its leader and published in Paris in 1586 by Martin Basanier at the urging of Richard Hakluyt. It describes the alliances and conflicts with the Timucua chiefs Saturiwa and Utina, the colony’s hunger and the Spanish attack of 1565.

fuentes/histoire-notable-de-la-floride/p.texto: It is the French version of the first struggle among European powers for Florida and an important source on the Timucua.

fuentes/brevis-narratio-le-moyne/titulo.texto: A Brief Narrative of What Happened to the French in Florida

fuentes/brevis-narratio-le-moyne/soporte.texto: Second part of Theodor de Bry’s America series, with 42 engravings

fuentes/brevis-narratio-le-moyne/resumen.texto: Account by the painter of Fort Caroline, published after his death by Theodor de Bry with engravings of the Timucua based on his drawings: their villages, crops, ceremonies, wars and treatment of dead enemies.

fuentes/brevis-narratio-le-moyne/por_que.texto: His images fixed in Europe the figure of the North American Indigenous person; historians debate how much De Bry added and how faithful the images are to what Le Moyne saw.

fuentes/brevis-narratio-le-moyne/leer.0..texto: English translation (Boston, 1875) with De Bry’s engravings, on Internet Archive

fuentes/discourse-of-western-planting/so.texto: Written for Elizabeth I and Walter Raleigh; unpublished until 1877

fuentes/discourse-of-western-planting/re.texto: Memorial listing the reasons for England to found colonies in North America: bringing the Gospel to the Indigenous peoples, opening markets for English wool, employing the poor and unemployed, gaining bases against Spain and curbing its power. It uses Las Casas’s accounts of Spanish cruelty as an argument for presenting the English as better colonizers.

fuentes/discourse-of-western-planting/po.texto: It is the program of the English colonial project and an early example of the use of the Black Legend in the rivalry among powers.

fuentes/briefe-and-true-report/titulo.texto: A Briefe and True Report of the New Found Land of Virginia

fuentes/briefe-and-true-report/soporte.texto: Reissued in 1590 by Theodor de Bry, in English, Latin, French and German, with engravings based on John White’s watercolors

fuentes/briefe-and-true-report/resumen.texto: Report on the Roanoke colony describing the land’s useful products, Indigenous crops (maize, beans, tobacco) and the society, religion and weapons of the Carolina Algonquians. It recounts that in the villages the English visited, many Indigenous people died of a disease that the English did not suffer from, and that the Indigenous people blamed the English for it.

fuentes/briefe-and-true-report/por_que_i.texto: It is the first published book about the first English colony in America, written to attract investors, and one of the earliest written accounts of a contact epidemic in the region.

fuentes/briefe-and-true-report/leer.0.ti.texto: Theodor de Bry edition (Frankfurt, 1590), with the engravings, on Internet Archive

fuentes/acuarelas-de-john-white/titulo.texto: John White’s Watercolors of Virginia and the Carolina Algonquians

fuentes/acuarelas-de-john-white/soporte.texto: About seventy-five watercolors held at the British Museum

fuentes/acuarelas-de-john-white/resumen.texto: Paintings made on the 1585 expedition showing the villages of Pomeiooc and Secotan, their houses and fields, ceremonies, fishing, ways of cooking and sitting, chiefs, women and children, as well as plants, fish and birds. They also include figures of Inuit from Frobisher’s expedition.

fuentes/acuarelas-de-john-white/por_que_.texto: They are the most direct representation of a North American Indigenous people in the 16th century; De Bry’s engravings that spread them altered them.

fuentes/generall-historie-smith/titulo.texto: The Generall Historie of Virginia, New England, and the Summer Isles

fuentes/generall-historie-smith/resumen.texto: History of the English colonies compiled by John Smith, with his own accounts and those of others. It narrates the first years of Jamestown, his capture by Opechancanough, the scene in which Pocahontas saves his life, relations with Powhatan, and the 1622 attack, which he presents as treachery that gave the English the right to conquer.

fuentes/generall-historie-smith/por_que_.texto: It is the most cited source on early Virginia, written by a protagonist who exalted his own role; episodes absent from his 1608 account are read with caution.

fuentes/generall-historie-smith/leer.0.t.texto: London edition of 1624, on Internet Archive

fuentes/mourts-relation/resumen.texto: Journal of the first months of the Plymouth colony: the exploration of Cape Cod, where the colonists took corn stored by Indigenous people and opened graves, the first winter, the arrival of Samoset and Squanto, and the treaty with Massasoit of March 1621. It includes Winslow’s letter describing the harvest of autumn 1621.

fuentes/mourts-relation/por_que_importa.texto: It is the only contemporary account of the 1621 celebration that was later called the “first Thanksgiving.”

fuentes/mourts-relation/leer.0.titulo.texto: Reprint by George B. Cheever (1848), on Internet Archive

fuentes/of-plymouth-plantation/soporte.texto: Complete manuscript published in 1856; returned by England to Massachusetts in 1897

fuentes/of-plymouth-plantation/resumen.texto: History of the Plymouth colony written by its governor, from the exile of the Separatists in Holland to 1647. It describes the land emptied by epidemic, the alliance with Massasoit and Squanto, the smallpox of 1634, and the Pequot War, whose Mystic massacre it narrates as a “sweet sacrifice” offered to God for victory.

fuentes/of-plymouth-plantation/por_que_i.texto: It is the founding work of New England historiography and a clear document of how the Puritans interpreted the deaths of Indigenous people as providence.

fuentes/of-plymouth-plantation/leer.0.ti.texto: Massachusetts Historical Society edition (1912), volume I, on Internet Archive

fuentes/newes-from-america/resumen.texto: Account of the Pequot War by one of the leaders of the attack on Mystic, with an engraving of the fort surrounded by two rings of attackers. It justifies the killing of women and children with the argument that “sometimes the Scripture declares that women and children must die with their parents,” and recounts that the allied Narragansetts criticized him because he “kills too many men.”

fuentes/newes-from-america/por_que_impor.texto: It is one of the two eyewitness accounts of the attack on Mystic and a key text in the debate about the violence of the Puritan colonies.

fuentes/newes-from-america/leer.0.titulo.texto: London edition of 1638, on Internet Archive

fuentes/brief-history-of-the-pequot-war/.texto: A Brief History of the Pequot War
Written around 1656 and published by Thomas Prince in Boston in 1736

Account of the Pequot War by the Connecticut commander. It narrates the burning of the Mystic fort, the pursuit of the survivors and the taking of prisoners, and presents the victory as the work of God, who had laughed at their enemies and made them “like a fiery oven.”
It is the main English-side testimony alongside Underhill’s; historians use it for the figures and the development of the attack.
Boston edition of 1736, on Internet Archive

fuentes/key-into-the-language-of-america.texto: A Key into the Language of America

Vocabulary and conversation manual of the Narragansett language, arranged by topic (food, travel, trade, religion, war), with observations on customs and verses that compare Indigenous people with the English, sometimes to the English disadvantage.

It is the first study published in English of an American Indigenous language and one of the most favorable works to Indigenous people of its time; Williams also wrote it to curb Massachusetts’s claims to Rhode Island land.
London edition of 1643, on Internet Archive

fuentes/biblia-de-eliot/soporte.texto: New Testament in 1661 and complete Bible in 1663, printed at the Cambridge press by Samuel Green and Marmaduke Johnson with the Nipmuc James Printer

fuentes/biblia-de-eliot/resumen.texto: Complete translation of the Bible into the Massachusett language made by John Eliot with Indigenous translators such as Job Nesutan and John Sassamon, funded by the Society for the Propagation of the Gospel in New England. About a thousand copies were printed; many were lost in King Philip’s War, and a second edition was made in 1685.

fuentes/biblia-de-eliot/por_que_importa.texto: It is the first complete Bible printed in the Americas and an essential source for the current revival of the Wampanoag language.

fuentes/biblia-de-eliot/leer.0.titulo.texto: Cambridge (Massachusetts) edition of 1663, on Internet Archive

fuentes/narrativa-de-rowlandson/titulo.texto: The Soveraignty and Goodness of God (Mary Rowlandson’s captivity narrative)

fuentes/narrativa-de-rowlandson/resumen.texto: Account of Mary Rowlandson’s eleven weeks of captivity among the enemies of the colonies during King Philip’s War, arranged in twenty “removes.” It describes the death of her wounded daughter, the hunger she shared with her captors, her work for the sachem Weetamoo, her encounter with Metacom and her ransom, all read as a trial sent by God.

fuentes/narrativa-de-rowlandson/por_que_.texto: It was one of the most widely read books in colonial New England and the model of the captivity narrative, which for two centuries fed the image of the Indigenous person as enemy.

fuentes/beschryvinge-van-nieuw-nederlant.texto: Description of the Dutch colony on the Hudson written by a lawyer who had lived there since 1641. It devotes extensive attention to the Lenape and Mohawk: their appearance, villages, agriculture, religion, government and way of making war; its author had already denounced Kieft’s government and war in the “Remonstrance” of 1649.
It is the main Dutch description of the peoples of the Hudson Valley and the lower Delaware; it was written to attract colonists.
Amsterdam edition of 1655, on Internet Archive

fuentes/narrative-of-the-late-massacres/.texto: A Narrative of the Late Massacres

Pamphlet by Franklin, published in January 1764, that narrates the killing of the twenty Conestoga, name by name, at the hands of the Paxton Boys in December 1763. It argues that punishing innocent Indigenous people for the crimes of others is the mark of barbarians, and compares the attackers with the peoples whom European tradition considered cruel.
It was the main contemporary denunciation of the massacre and a document of the clash between the frontier and the Philadelphia elite.
Philadelphia edition of 1764, on Internet Archive

fuentes/cartas-de-amherst-y-bouquet/titu.texto: Letters between Jeffery Amherst and Henry Bouquet about smallpox

fuentes/cartas-de-amherst-y-bouquet/sopo.texto: Preserved among the Bouquet Papers at the British Library

fuentes/cartas-de-amherst-y-bouquet/resu.texto: Exchange of July 1763 during Pontiac’s Rebellion. In a postscript, Amherst asks whether it would not be possible to “send smallpox” among the discontented tribes; Bouquet replies that he will try to inoculate them with blankets, and Amherst approves the idea and suggests other methods to “extirpate this execrable race.”

fuentes/cartas-de-amherst-y-bouquet/por_.texto: They prove the intention to use smallpox as a weapon in the British high command; no document shows that this plan was carried out, apart from the June episode at Fort Pitt.

fuentes/cartas-de-amherst-y-bouquet/leer.texto: Transcription and images of the letters, gathered by Peter d’Errico on the University of Massachusetts website

fuentes/diario-de-william-trent/titulo.texto: Journal of William Trent at Fort Pitt

fuentes/diario-de-william-trent/soporte.texto: Published by A. T. Volwiler in the Mississippi Valley Historical Review in 1924

fuentes/diario-de-william-trent/resumen.texto: Journal of the siege of Fort Pitt from May to August 1763. In the entry for June 24 it records that two blankets and a handkerchief from the smallpox hospital were given to two Delawares who came to parley, in the hope that they would have “the desired effect.”

fuentes/diario-de-william-trent/por_que_.texto: Together with the invoice the army paid for those items, it is the only document of a deliberate gift of smallpox-contaminated objects to Indigenous people in British North America.

fuentes/proclamacion-real-de-1763/resume.texto: Proclamation of October 7, 1763 that organized the territories gained from France. It reserved for Indigenous peoples, under the protection of the Crown, the lands west of the Appalachian divide, prohibited colonists from settling there, and established that only the Crown could buy Indigenous lands, at public assemblies.

fuentes/proclamacion-real-de-1763/por_qu.texto: It was one of the colonists’ grievances that led to independence, and it remains the basis of Indigenous law in Canada, where it is cited in the Constitution of 1982.

fuentes/proclamacion-real-de-1763/leer.1.texto: Text on the Avalon Project at Yale University

fuentes/tratado-de-fort-stanwix-1768/res.texto: Deed of cession signed in November 1768 by the chiefs of the Six Nations before William Johnson. It moves the Proclamation line westward and cedes to the Crown the lands south of the Ohio River, which the Shawnees, Delawares and Cherokees also claimed, and who did not sign.

fuentes/tratado-de-fort-stanwix-1768/por.texto: It opened Kentucky and western Virginia and Pennsylvania to settlers and was one of the causes of Dunmore’s War of 1774.

fuentes/declaracion-de-independencia-de-.texto: Declaration of Independence of the United States

Declaration approved by the Continental Congress on July 4, 1776, drafted mainly by Jefferson. It affirms that all men are created equal, with unalienable rights to life, liberty and the pursuit of happiness, and lists the grievances against George III; the last accuses him of having incited against the inhabitants of the frontiers “the merciless Indian Savages,” whose mode of warfare is the destruction of all ages, sexes and conditions.
It is the birth certificate of the United States, the first independent state in the Americas; the grievance against the Indians shows how the colonists saw the peoples who opposed their advance.
Text on the Avalon Project at Yale University

fuentes/tratado-de-paris-1783/autor.texto: Great Britain and the United States

fuentes/tratado-de-paris-1783/resumen.texto: Treaty signed on September 3, 1783, by which Great Britain recognized the independence of the United States, with boundaries reaching the Mississippi to the west and the Great Lakes to the north. It does not mention the Indigenous peoples, many of them British allies, whose lands fell within those borders.

fuentes/tratado-de-paris-1783/por_que_im.texto: It ended the War of Independence; for the peoples of the Ohio and the Great Lakes, who had not been defeated, it was a cession made behind their backs that led to the Northwest Indian War.

fuentes/tratado-de-paris-1783/leer.0.tit.texto: Text on the Avalon Project at Yale University

fuentes/ordenanza-del-noroeste/resumen.texto: Law of July 13, 1787 that organized the territory north of the Ohio, provided for its division into future states equal to the original ones, and prohibited slavery there. Its third article states that “the utmost good faith” shall always be observed toward the Indians, that their lands shall not be taken without their consent except in “just and lawful wars authorized by Congress.”

fuentes/ordenanza-del-noroeste/por_que_i.texto: It was the model for the expansion of the United States; its promise to Indigenous peoples coexisted with the sale of those same lands to settlers and speculators.

fuentes/ordenanza-del-noroeste/leer.0.ti.texto: Text on the Avalon Project at Yale University

fuentes/notes-on-the-state-of-virginia/t.texto: Notes on the State of Virginia

fuentes/notes-on-the-state-of-virginia/r.texto: Jefferson’s answer to a French questionnaire about Virginia, printed in Paris in 1785. It refutes Buffon and Raynal, who argued that American nature degenerated animals and people, with data on the fauna and with Logan’s speech as proof of Indigenous eloquence; it describes his excavation of a burial mound and lists the peoples of Virginia. In the same book he raises, “as a suspicion,” the inferiority of Africans.

fuentes/notes-on-the-state-of-virginia/p.texto: It is a key text of the American Enlightenment on Indigenous peoples and of its contradiction with slavery; his excavation is cited as one of the first to use stratigraphic method.

fuentes/notes-on-the-state-of-virginia/l.texto: London edition of 1787, on Internet Archive

fuentes/tratado-de-canandaigua/autor.texto: Timothy Pickering and the chiefs of the Six Nations

fuentes/tratado-de-canandaigua/resumen.texto: Treaty of November 11, 1794 between the United States and the Six Nations, signed by Cornplanter, Red Jacket and other chiefs. It recognizes the lands of the Seneca and other nations in New York, which the United States commits not to claim, and sets an annual payment in cloth that is still delivered.

fuentes/tratado-de-canandaigua/por_que_i.texto: It is one of the oldest treaties still in force between the United States and Indigenous nations.

fuentes/tratado-de-canandaigua/leer.0.ti.texto: Text on the Avalon Project at Yale University

fuentes/tratado-de-greenville/autor.texto: Anthony Wayne and the chiefs of twelve Northwest nations

fuentes/tratado-de-greenville/resumen.texto: Treaty of August 3, 1795, signed after the Battle of Fallen Timbers by Anthony Wayne and more than ninety chiefs of the Wyandots, Delawares, Shawnees, Odawas, Ojibwes, Potawatomis, Miamis and others. They ceded most of present-day Ohio in exchange for goods worth $20,000 and annual payments of $9,500.

fuentes/tratado-de-greenville/por_que_im.texto: It ended the Northwest Indian War and set a line that settlers crossed within a few years; it was one of the reasons for Tecumseh’s confederacy.

fuentes/tratado-de-greenville/leer.0.tit.texto: Text on the Avalon Project at Yale University

fuentes/indian-removal-act/resumen.texto: Law of May 28, 1830 that authorized the president to exchange the lands of the Indigenous peoples of the East for lands west of the Mississippi, pay them for their improvements, and cover the cost of their removal. It says that the peoples could choose, and guarantees the new lands “forever.”

fuentes/indian-removal-act/por_que_impor.texto: It was the legal basis for the forced removals of the Choctaws, Creeks, Chickasaws, Cherokees, Seminoles and northern peoples in the following two decades.

fuentes/cherokee-nation-v-georgia/resume.texto: Supreme Court ruling of March 18, 1831 that dismissed the Cherokee Nation’s suit against Georgia’s laws for lack of jurisdiction. Marshall’s opinion defines Indigenous peoples as “domestic dependent nations,” whose relation to the United States resembles that of a ward to his guardian.

fuentes/cherokee-nation-v-georgia/por_qu.texto: That definition remains the basis of the status of Indigenous nations in United States law.

fuentes/worcester-v-georgia/resumen.texto: Supreme Court ruling of March 3, 1832 that overturned Georgia’s conviction of the missionary Samuel Worcester for living without a permit in Cherokee territory. It held that the Cherokee Nation was a distinct community in which Georgia’s laws had no force, and that only the federal government could deal with it.

fuentes/worcester-v-georgia/por_que_impo.texto: It recognized Cherokee sovereignty against the states, but neither Georgia nor President Jackson enforced it, and the removal went ahead.

fuentes/cherokee-phoenix/resumen.texto: Weekly newspaper of the Cherokee Nation, the first of a North American Indigenous people, printed in New Echota in English and in Sequoyah’s syllabary. It published the nation’s laws, news, and the Cherokees’ defense against Georgia and the removal policy.

fuentes/cherokee-phoenix/por_que_importa.texto: It shows an Indigenous nation with a written constitution, press and its own literacy at the very time it was accused of not being “civilized” as a justification for its removal.

fuentes/ley-de-proteccion-de-los-indios-.texto: An Act for the Government and Protection of Indians (California, 1850)

Law of April 22, 1850 that allowed white people to take Indigenous minors into their custody with the permission of a justice of the peace, and that Indigenous people accused of vagrancy be leased to the highest bidder for up to four months. It prohibited convicting a white person solely on the testimony of an Indigenous person.
Under a protective name, it gave legal form to a system of forced labor and the trafficking of Indigenous children; its main articles were repealed in 1863.

fuentes/mensaje-de-burnett-1851/titulo.texto: Message of Governor Burnett to the California Legislature (1851)

fuentes/mensaje-de-burnett-1851/resumen.texto: Annual message to the legislature of January 1851. On Indigenous people, it states that a “war of extermination” between the races must be expected to continue until the Indian race is extinct, and that, although it is to be lamented, preventing it is beyond the power or wisdom of man.

fuentes/mensaje-de-burnett-1851/por_que_.texto: It is the most used quotation to argue that the California killings had official backing; those who dispute the genocide thesis read it as a prediction and not as an order.

fuentes/diario-de-steller/titulo.texto: Journal of the Voyage with Bering

fuentes/diario-de-steller/soporte.texto: Published by Peter Simon Pallas in 1793; English translation by Frank Golder in 1925

fuentes/diario-de-steller/resumen.texto: Journal of the naturalist of Bering’s expedition describing the landing on Kayak Island, the first observations of Alaskan plants, birds and mammals, the encounter with people of the Shumagin Islands, the shipwreck on Bering Island, the scurvy and the life of the survivors, who ate sea otters, seals and sea cows.

fuentes/diario-de-steller/por_que_import.texto: It is the main source on the first Russian contact with Alaska; his report on the abundance of sea otters opened the fur trade.

fuentes/viaje-de-shelikhov/titulo.texto: Voyage of Grigori Shelikhov from Okhotsk to the American Coast

fuentes/viaje-de-shelikhov/resumen.texto: Account of the 1783–1786 expedition that founded the settlement of Three Saints Bay on Kodiak. It describes the Alutiiq, their houses and customs, and presents the island’s submission as peaceful, without mentioning the attack on Awa’uq that Russian and Indigenous witnesses later denounced.

fuentes/viaje-de-shelikhov/por_que_impor.texto: It is the account of Russian America’s own founder, written to obtain a trade monopoly; it is to be contrasted with the denunciations that led to investigating him.

fuentes/viaje-de-shelikhov/leer.0.titulo.texto: English translation of 1795, facsimile from Canadiana on Internet Archive

fuentes/the-spanish-frontier-in-north-am.texto: The Spanish Frontier in North America

Synthesis of the Spanish presence from Florida to California between 1513 and 1821: expeditions, missions, presidios, trade, relations with Indigenous peoples and with the other powers. It treats with equal care the violence of the conquest and the forced labor in the missions, and the protective policies and diplomacy of the Bourbon frontier.

It is the standard reference on the subject; it broke with the view that saw the history of the United States only from the English colonies, without falling into the idealization of the “Spanish frontier” of Herbert Bolton’s school.

fuentes/children-of-coyote/titulo.texto: Children of Coyote, Missionaries of Saint Francis

fuentes/children-of-coyote/resumen.texto: Study of the Mission San Carlos and the Monterey region based on baptism, marriage and burial records. It reconstructs the demographic collapse of the coastal peoples (through disease, high infant mortality and low birth rates), labor, punishments, escapes, and the participation of Indigenous people in mission government as alcaldes.

fuentes/children-of-coyote/por_que_impor.texto: It is one of the most cited studies of the California mission system and shows both its demographic cost and the capacity of Indigenous people to adapt and negotiate within it.

fuentes/the-indian-slave-trade-gallay/ti.texto: The Indian Slave Trade: The Rise of the English Empire in the American South, 1670–1717

fuentes/the-indian-slave-trade-gallay/re.texto: Studies how Carolina merchants bought captives of other peoples from their Indigenous allies to sell them as slaves, and estimates that between 1670 and 1715 between 24,000 and 51,000 people were sold. It shows how that trade destroyed the Spanish missions, remade the alliances of the Southeast and ended with the Yamasee War.

fuentes/the-indian-slave-trade-gallay/po.texto: It placed Indigenous slavery at the center of the colonial history of the Southeast; it won the Bancroft Prize in 2003.

fuentes/biological-warfare-fenn-2000/tit.texto: Biological Warfare in Eighteenth-Century North America: Beyond Jeffery Amherst

fuentes/biological-warfare-fenn-2000/res.texto: Gathers the documented cases of intent or attempt to spread smallpox in the North American wars of the 18th century, from Fort Pitt to the War of Independence, and distinguishes them from rumors. It concludes that intent is proven in several cases, that effectiveness cannot be verified, and that the idea was acceptable to many contemporaries.

fuentes/biological-warfare-fenn-2000/por.texto: It is the standard review of the episode of the blankets and of its documentary limits.

fuentes/ranlet-2000/titulo.texto: The British, the Indians, and Smallpox: What Actually Happened at Fort Pitt in 1763

fuentes/ranlet-2000/resumen.texto: Analyzes the Fort Pitt documents and argues that smallpox was already circulating among the peoples of the Ohio before the blankets were handed out, that the two Delawares who received them remained alive months later, and that there is no proof that they caused the epidemic.

fuentes/ranlet-2000/por_que_importa.texto: It is the main skeptical argument against the idea that the Fort Pitt blankets caused an epidemic.

fuentes/the-middle-ground/resumen.texto: Studies how the French and the Great Lakes peoples, refugees from the Iroquois wars, built a “middle ground” of alliances, gifts, trade and useful misunderstandings, in which neither could impose itself by force. It follows its crisis with the British, Pontiac’s Rebellion and its end with the expansion of the United States.

fuentes/the-middle-ground/por_que_import.texto: It changed the way relations between Europeans and Indigenous peoples were studied, which ceased to be seen only as conquest or resistance; its concept has been applied to other frontiers.

fuentes/facing-east-from-indian-country/.texto: Tells the history of colonial North America from the point of view of Indigenous peoples, starting from episodes such as the arrival of the Europeans as seen from the villages, the lives of Pocahontas or Metacom, and the Revolution, which for many peoples was a defeat.
It is a widely used synthesis of colonial-era Indigenous history, based on European documents read against the grain and on archaeology.

fuentes/war-and-culture-richter/titulo.texto: War and Culture: The Iroquois Experience

fuentes/war-and-culture-richter/resumen.texto: Argues that the Iroquois wars of the 17th century were largely “mourning wars”: raids to take captives who would replace the dead, who were adopted into families or tortured and executed in public rites. Epidemics multiplied these wars, which were mixed with competition for furs.

fuentes/war-and-culture-richter/por_que_.texto: It is the classic article on the Indigenous logic of war in the Northeast, against the purely economic explanation of the beaver wars.

fuentes/an-american-genocide/resumen.texto: Reconstructs from contemporary documents the killings of California Indigenous people between 1846 and 1873, with an appendix on each case, and estimates between about 9,500 and 16,000 deaths by homicide. It documents state and federal payments to militias, the forced labor laws and the speeches calling for extermination, and argues that it was a genocide under the 1948 UN convention.

fuentes/an-american-genocide/por_que_imp.texto: It is the central work in the debate on the California genocide; its critics accept most of the data but dispute the state’s intent and whether deaths from disease and hunger should be counted.

fuentes/the-name-of-war/resumen.texto: Studies King Philip’s War through what was written about it: chronicles, sermons, Rowlandson’s narrative, letters from literate Indigenous people, and its memory up to the 19th century. It shows how the colonists used words to present their own acts as civilized and those of the Indigenous people as savage.

fuentes/the-name-of-war/por_que_importa.texto: It won the Bancroft Prize in 1999 and is one of the most widely read works on the war.

fuentes/the-invasion-of-america/resumen.texto: Critique of the traditional historiography of New England, which presented the Puritans as civilizers facing “savages.” It argues that the English colonies advanced through conquest and dispossession, presented in the language of virtue, and it reinterprets the Pequot and King Philip’s wars.

fuentes/the-invasion-of-america/por_que_.texto: It was very influential in the critical turn of colonial history in the 1970s; it is criticized for its polemical tone and overly harsh judgments of the Puritans.

fuentes/when-jesus-came-gutierrez/titulo.texto: When Jesus Came, the Corn Mothers Went Away

fuentes/when-jesus-came-gutierrez/resume.texto: History of New Mexico through marriage, sexuality and honor, from the peoples before the conquest to 1846. It interprets the Franciscan mission as a clash of systems of authority and explains the 1680 revolt and the society of genízaros and castes.

fuentes/when-jesus-came-gutierrez/por_qu.texto: It has won many awards and has also been strongly criticized by a group of Pueblo intellectuals, who objected that it used Spanish sources to speak about their religion and sexuality without consulting them.

fuentes/the-children-of-aataentsic/resum.texto: History of the Hurons from archaeology to their dispersal in 1649–1650, which combines excavations with a critical reading of Champlain, Sagard and the Jesuit Relations. It estimates their population before the epidemics and analyzes how the fur trade, epidemics and the mission weakened them against the Iroquois.

fuentes/the-children-of-aataentsic/por_q.texto: It is the classic work of Northeastern ethnohistory, which treated the Hurons as subjects of their own history.

fuentes/marr-cathey-2010/titulo.texto: A New Hypothesis for the Cause of an Epidemic among Native Americans, New England, 1616–1619

fuentes/marr-cathey-2010/autor.texto: John S. Marr and John T. Cathey

fuentes/marr-cathey-2010/resumen.texto: Reviews the descriptions of the epidemic that depopulated the New England coast before the arrival of the Plymouth colonists and rules out plague, smallpox and yellow fever. It proposes leptospirosis, worsened by the arrival of European rats.

fuentes/marr-cathey-2010/por_que_importa.texto: It is the most recent hypothesis about an epidemic that was decisive for English colonization, whose cause is still not known with certainty.

fuentes/marr-cathey-2010/leer.0.titulo.texto: Article in Emerging Infectious Diseases, the open-access journal of the CDC

fuentes/cook-1943/titulo.texto: The Conflict between the California Indian and White Civilization

fuentes/cook-1943/resumen.texto: Demographic study of California’s Indigenous people that uses mission records to measure mortality, birth rates, food, labor and punishments in the mission system, and then the impact of the gold rush. Cook later revised his figures (1976): about 310,000 Indigenous people in 1769, about 150,000 in 1848 and about 30,000 in 1870.

fuentes/cook-1943/por_que_importa.texto: It founded the quantitative study of California Indigenous demography, and its figures remain the starting point of the debate.

personas/hernando-de-soto/resumen.texto: Conquistador from Extremadura who took part in the conquest of Nicaragua and Peru, where he was at Cajamarca in 1532. With his share of Peruvian wealth he obtained from Charles V the governorship of Florida, and between 1539 and 1542 he traveled with about 600 men through the chiefdoms of the present-day southeastern United States, taking maize, carriers and women; he died of fever on the Mississippi in May 1542.

personas/tascalusa/resumen.texto: Chief of a Mississippian chiefdom in present-day Alabama, described by the chroniclers of the de Soto expedition as a very tall and haughty man. Held as a hostage by de Soto, he took him to the fortified town of Mabila, where his warriors attacked the Spaniards in October 1540; what became of him after the battle is not known.

personas/pedro-menendez-de-aviles/resume.texto: Seaman from Asturias, captain general of the Indies fleet, who founded St. Augustine in 1565, took the Huguenot colony of Fort Caroline, and had some 245 shipwrecked French sailors who had surrendered executed at Matanzas. He attempted a network of forts and Jesuit missions from Florida to Chesapeake Bay and died in Santander while preparing a fleet.

personas/juan-pardo/resumen.texto: Captain sent by Menéndez de Avilés from Santa Elena who, in two expeditions (1566–1568), traveled the interior of the Carolinas and eastern Tennessee and left six forts with small garrisons, all destroyed by Indigenous people around 1568. Excavations at the Berry site in North Carolina found Fort San Juan next to the village of Joara.

personas/lucas-vazquez-de-ayllon/activo..texto: San Miguel de Gualdape (Georgia coast, uncertain site)

personas/lucas-vazquez-de-ayllon/resumen.texto: Oidor of the Audiencia of Santo Domingo whose ships captured about sixty Indigenous people on the South Carolina coast in 1521. In 1526 he took some 600 settlers, with enslaved Africans, to found San Miguel de Gualdape, the first attempt at European settlement in the mainland territory of present-day United States; he died there and the colony was abandoned within a few months.

personas/tristan-de-luna/resumen.texto: Veteran of the Coronado expedition who in 1559 took some 1,500 people to settle Pensacola Bay. A hurricane sank most of his fleet within a few weeks, and the colony was abandoned in 1561.

personas/estebanico/resumen.texto: African enslaved man born in Azemmour (Morocco), owned by Andrés Dorantes. He was one of the four survivors of the Narváez expedition who crossed the southern part of North America to reach Mexico in 1536. In 1539 he went ahead as a guide for Fray Marcos de Niza, and the Zuni of Hawikuh killed him.

personas/marcos-de-niza/resumen.texto: Franciscan born in Nice, then part of Savoy, who had been in Peru. In 1539 Viceroy Mendoza sent him north with Estebanico, and his report claimed he had seen from a distance the city of Cíbola, “greater than the city of Mexico”; when the Coronado expedition found the Zuni village of Hawikuh in 1540, the soldiers accused him of having lied.

personas/francisco-vazquez-de-coronado/r.texto: Governor of Nueva Galicia who in 1540–1542 led an expedition of some 350 Spaniards and more than a thousand Indigenous allies from central Mexico in search of the cities of Cíbola. He reached the Zuni villages, the Rio Grande and the plains of Kansas without finding riches; in the 1544 inquiry into the expedition’s abuses he was acquitted.

personas/pedro-de-castaneda-de-najera/re.texto: Soldier of the Coronado expedition, a resident of Culiacán, who some twenty years later wrote the “Relación de la jornada de Cíbola.” Beyond what his own text says, little is known about him.

personas/juan-de-onate/activo.lugar.texto: Ohkay Owingeh (San Juan de los Caballeros)

personas/juan-de-onate/resumen.texto: Son of a wealthy silver miner from Zacatecas, married to a descendant of Cortés and Moctezuma. In 1598 he brought settlers, soldiers, Franciscans and livestock to New Mexico and became its first governor; after the capture of Acoma (1599) he sentenced the men over 25 years old to amputation of a foot and to servitude. In 1614 he was convicted in Mexico for these and other abuses, among other penalties being banished from New Mexico.

personas/gaspar-perez-de-villagra/activo.texto: Ohkay Owingeh (San Juan de los Caballeros)

personas/gaspar-perez-de-villagra/resume.texto: Creole from Puebla who studied in Salamanca and was a captain and procurator of the Oñate expedition. He fought in the capture of Acoma and published in 1610 the “Historia de la Nueva México,” an epic poem in 34 cantos; in 1614 he was convicted for the execution of two deserters.

personas/pope-pueblo/resumen.texto: Tewa religious leader from Ohkay Owingeh. In 1675 he was among the 47 Pueblo men arrested and whipped for “sorcery” on the orders of Governor Treviño; from Taos he organized the revolt of August 1680. According to the testimony gathered by Otermín, he ordered the destruction of churches, images and rosaries and the abandonment of Christian names; after the victory he lost the support of the peoples and died before the Spanish returned.

personas/alonso-de-benavides/resumen.texto: Franciscan born in the Azores, custodian of the New Mexico missions from 1626 to 1629. His Memorial to the King (1630) describes the missions and the Indigenous peoples for the purposes of missionary propaganda; after meeting with her in 1631, he spread the account of the nun María de Ágreda, who was said to have preached to the Jumanos without leaving Spain.

personas/antonio-de-otermin/resumen.texto: Governor of New Mexico during the 1680 revolt. He resisted the siege of Santa Fe, evacuated the survivors to El Paso and failed in an attempt at reconquest in 1681–1682; his proceedings, with interrogations of captive Indians, are the main source on the revolt.

personas/diego-de-vargas/resumen.texto: Nobleman from Madrid, governor of New Mexico, who entered Santa Fe without combat in 1692 and in December 1693 took it by assault, after which he had some seventy defenders executed and distributed about four hundred women and children as servants. He suppressed another Pueblo revolt in 1696.

personas/gaspar-de-portola/resumen.texto: Catalan military officer, governor of the Californias, who in 1767–1768 carried out the expulsion of the Jesuits from Baja California and in 1769–1770 led the overland expedition that founded San Diego and Monterey.

personas/junipero-serra/muerte.lugar.texto: Mission San Carlos Borromeo de Carmelo

personas/junipero-serra/activo.lugar.texto: Mission San Carlos Borromeo de Carmelo

personas/junipero-serra/resumen.texto: Franciscan from Mallorca, professor of theology in Palma, who did missionary work in the Sierra Gorda of Querétaro and from 1769 in Alta California, where he founded nine missions and presided over the system until his death. In 1773 he obtained from the viceroy that the missionaries, and not the soldiers, have authority over the baptized Indians, and in a letter (1780) he defended the whipping of neophytes as a father’s punishment of his children. He was beatified in 1988 and canonized in 2015, despite opposition from California Indigenous groups.

personas/francisco-palou/resumen.texto: Franciscan from Mallorca, Serra’s disciple in Palma, who accompanied him in the Sierra Gorda and in California, where in 1776 he founded the Mission San Francisco. He wrote the “Relación histórica” of Serra’s life (1787), the basis of his later image.

personas/fermin-lasuen/muerte.lugar.texto: Mission San Carlos Borromeo de Carmelo

personas/fermin-lasuen/activo.lugar.texto: Mission San Carlos Borromeo de Carmelo

personas/fermin-lasuen/resumen.texto: Serra’s successor as president of the Alta California missions (1785–1803), he founded nine more. In 1801 he refuted in writing the accusations of the Franciscan Antonio de la Concepción Horra, who in 1798 had charged that the system treated the neophytes cruelly.

personas/toypurina/resumen.texto: Tongva woman considered a sorceress by her own people, who in October 1785 took part, with the neophyte Nicolás José, in a plan to attack Mission San Gabriel. When the plan was discovered, she was tried and banished to Mission San Carlos, where she was baptized and married a Spanish soldier; the most quoted line of her testimony, against those who lived on her land, comes from a 1958 novelized version and not from the case file.

personas/juan-bautista-de-anza/resumen.texto: Creole military officer from Sonora who opened an overland route to California in 1774 and in 1775–1776 led about 240 settlers who founded San Francisco. As governor of New Mexico he defeated the Comanche chief Cuerno Verde in 1779, and in 1786 he signed a peace with the Comanches with Ecueracapa.

personas/bernardo-de-galvez/resumen.texto: Governor of Spanish Louisiana who, in the American War of Independence, took Baton Rouge, Mobile and Pensacola from the British (1779–1781). As viceroy of New Spain he signed the “Instrucción” of 1786 for the northern frontier, which ordered war against hostile Apaches and made those who asked for peace dependent through gifts, alcohol and poor-quality weapons.

personas/jacques-cartier/resumen.texto: Navigator from Saint-Malo who made three voyages to the Gulf and the Saint Lawrence River (1534, 1535–1536 and 1541–1542). He reached the Iroquoian villages of Stadacona and Hochelaga, took the chief Donnacona and nine others to France, where they died, and spread the name “Canada,” from the Iroquoian word for village.

personas/donnacona/resumen.texto: Chief of the Iroquoian village of Stadacona, on the site of present-day Quebec City. Cartier took two of his sons to France in 1534 and him, with nine others, in 1536; he died in France around 1539 without having returned.

personas/samuel-de-champlain/resumen.texto: Navigator and cartographer from Brouage who founded Quebec in 1608 and governed it until his death, except during the English occupation of 1629–1632. He allied with the Montagnais, Algonquins and Hurons against the Iroquois League and in 1609 killed two Mohawk chiefs with his arquebus by the lake that bears his name; his accounts and maps are a basic source on the peoples of the Saint Lawrence and the Great Lakes.

personas/gabriel-sagard/resumen.texto: Lay brother of the Recollects who lived among the Hurons in 1623–1624. His “Grand voyage du pays des Hurons” (1632) describes his life, beliefs and wars and includes a dictionary of the Huron language.

personas/paul-le-jeune/resumen.texto: Superior of the Jesuits in New France from 1632, who began the annual series of the Relations. He spent the winter of 1633–1634 with a band of Montagnais (Innu) to learn their language and recounted it in the 1634 Relation, one of the most detailed descriptions of a northern hunting people.

personas/jean-de-brebeuf/resumen.texto: Jesuit from Normandy who lived among the Hurons from 1626, learned their language, wrote a catechism in it and drafted parts of the Relations. The Iroquois captured him during the destruction of the Huron villages in March 1649, and he died under ritual torture; he was canonized in 1930 among the “Canadian Martyrs.”

personas/marie-de-l-incarnation/resumen.texto: Ursuline from Tours, a widow and mother of a son, who arrived in Quebec in 1639 and founded the Ursuline convent and school for French and Indigenous girls. She wrote dictionaries and catechisms in Algonquin, Montagnais and Iroquois, now lost, and thousands of letters, of which her son published a selection in 1681; she was canonized in 2014.

personas/francois-de-laval/resumen.texto: First bishop of Quebec (apostolic vicar from 1658 and bishop from 1674), who founded the Seminary of Quebec in 1663. He fought the sale of alcohol to Indigenous people with excommunications, in conflict with governors and merchants.

personas/kateri-tekakwitha/resumen.texto: Mohawk woman, daughter of a Christian Algonquin, who as a child survived a smallpox epidemic with her face scarred. Baptized by the Jesuits in 1676, she moved to the Kahnawake mission near Montreal, where she practiced extreme penances and died at 24; she was canonized in 2012, the first Indigenous person from present-day United States or Canada to be raised to the altars as a saint.

personas/jacques-marquette/resumen.texto: French Jesuit who did missionary work among the Hurons and Odawas of the Great Lakes and in 1673 traveled the Mississippi with Louis Jolliet as far as the mouth of the Arkansas. He died in 1675 on his way back from a mission among the Illinois.

personas/louis-jolliet/resumen.texto: Merchant and cartographer born in Quebec and educated by the Jesuits, who in 1673 traveled the Mississippi with Marquette and confirmed that it flowed into the Gulf of Mexico.

personas/la-salle/resumen.texto: Merchant and explorer from Rouen who in 1682 descended the Mississippi to the Gulf and took possession of its entire basin for Louis XIV, naming it Louisiana. In 1685 he landed by mistake on the Texas coast with about 300 settlers, and he was murdered by his own men in 1687.

personas/kondiaronk/resumen.texto: Wendat (Huron-Petun) chief of Michilimackinac, called “Le Rat” by the French. He was one of the main negotiators of the Great Peace of Montreal and died there during the 1701 conferences. Baron de Lahontan took him as the model of the Indigenous person who criticizes Europe in his “Dialogues” (1703), though how faithfully they reflect his ideas is doubtful.

personas/bienville/resumen.texto: Born in Montreal, he was governor of French Louisiana in several periods and founded New Orleans in 1718. Under his government the Code Noir of Louisiana (1724) was enacted, and the wars against the Natchez and the Chickasaws were fought.

personas/le-page-du-pratz/resumen.texto: French colonist who lived for about eight years near the Natchez before the 1729 rebellion and learned their language. His “Histoire de la Louisiane” (1758) describes their society, religion and the human sacrifices at the funerals of the nobility.

personas/jacques-le-moyne/resumen.texto: Huguenot painter who was at Fort Caroline and escaped in 1565. Theodor de Bry published engravings in 1591 based on his drawings of the Timucua, together with his account; only one original painting of Florida survives, and the fidelity of the engravings is disputed.

personas/rene-de-laudonniere/resumen.texto: Huguenot who founded Fort Caroline in 1564, on the land of the Timucua chief Saturiwa, and survived the Spanish attack of 1565. His “Histoire notable de la Floride” (1586) narrates the colony and its relations with the Timucua chiefs.

personas/jean-ribault/resumen.texto: Huguenot navigator from Dieppe who in 1562 built Charlesfort at Port Royal and in 1565 brought reinforcements to Fort Caroline. His fleet was wrecked in a hurricane as he was about to attack St. Augustine, and Menéndez de Avilés had him executed at Matanzas along with most of his men.

personas/richard-hakluyt/resumen.texto: English clergyman and geographer who gathered travel accounts in “The Principall Navigations” (1589) and in 1584 wrote a discourse for the queen in favor of colonizing North America, with religious, commercial and rivalry-with-Spain arguments, whose cruelty toward the Indians he cited according to Las Casas.

personas/thomas-hariot/resumen.texto: Mathematician and astronomer in the service of Walter Raleigh who was at Roanoke in 1585–1586, learned part of the Carolina Algonquian language with Manteo and Wanchese, and wrote the “Briefe and True Report” (1588). In 1609 he drew the Moon as observed through a telescope, months before Galileo.

personas/john-white-pintor/resumen.texto: English painter and cartographer who accompanied the 1585 expedition and left dozens of watercolors of the Carolina Algonquians, the most important visual source on them. He was governor of the colony from 1587; when he returned in 1590 he found it abandoned.

personas/powhatan/resumen.texto: Paramount chief of a confederacy of some thirty Algonquian-speaking communities on the Virginia coast, which he had inherited and expanded through conquest; according to William Strachey he had the Chesapeake destroyed around 1607. He traded and fought with the English of Jamestown; the marriage of his daughter Pocahontas to John Rolfe (1614) opened a truce that lasted until his death.

personas/pocahontas/resumen.texto: Daughter of Powhatan. In 1613 the English took her hostage to negotiate with her father; in captivity she was baptized with the name Rebecca and in 1614 she married the colonist John Rolfe. She traveled to England in 1616 as propaganda for the Virginia Company and died in Gravesend in 1617, as she was beginning the return voyage.

personas/opechancanough/resumen.texto: Brother or relative of Powhatan and his de facto successor, who led the coordinated attacks of 1622 and 1644 against the Virginia colonists. Captured in 1646 when very old, he was shot by a soldier while in custody in Jamestown.

personas/john-smith/resumen.texto: English soldier who had fought against the Ottomans, a member of the Jamestown council and its president in 1608–1609. He mapped Chesapeake Bay and obtained maize from the Powhatan through barter and threats. The scene in which Pocahontas saves his life is not in his 1608 account: it appears in a letter he wrote in 1616 to Queen Anne, which he himself published in the “Generall Historie” of 1624; historians debate whether it happened or was an adoption rite that he did not understand.

personas/squanto/resumen.texto: Patuxet captured in 1614 by the English captain Thomas Hunt and sold as a slave in Málaga; he went to England and returned to New England in 1619, when the epidemic had emptied his village. He served as interpreter for the Plymouth colonists and as mediator with Massasoit until his death from fever in 1622.

personas/massasoit/resumen.texto: Principal sachem of the Wampanoag, whose people had been decimated by the 1616–1619 epidemic. In March 1621 he signed with the Plymouth colonists an alliance of mutual aid, partly against the Narragansetts, his rivals, which he maintained until his death.

personas/metacom/muerte.lugar.texto: Rhode Island and Providence Plantations colony

personas/metacom/resumen.texto: Son of Massasoit and sachem of the Wampanoag from 1662, called “King Philip” by the English. He led the 1675–1676 war against the New England colonies; he died in August 1676 at the hands of an Indigenous man allied with the English, his head was displayed in Plymouth for about twenty years, and his nine-year-old son was sold into slavery outside the colony.

personas/uncas/resumen.texto: Mohegan sachem, separate from the Pequots, who allied with the English in the Pequot War and fought at Mystic. In 1643 he captured the Narragansett sachem Miantonomi and executed him with the approval of the colonial commissioners; he was also an ally of Connecticut in King Philip’s War.

personas/john-sassamon/resumen.texto: Christian Massachusett, interpreter for John Eliot and for a time a student at Harvard, who became a scribe for Metacom. In January 1675 he was found dead in a frozen pond after warning Plymouth that Metacom was preparing war; the execution of three Wampanoag for his death precipitated King Philip’s War.

personas/william-bradford/resumen.texto: English Separatist who arrived on the Mayflower and governed the Plymouth colony almost without interruption from 1621 to 1657. His history “Of Plymouth Plantation” narrates the colony up to 1647, including the alliance with Massasoit and the Pequot War.

personas/john-winthrop/resumen.texto: Puritan lawyer who led the 1630 fleet of the Massachusetts Bay Company and served as its governor for twelve years. In a 1634 letter he interpreted the deaths of Indigenous people from smallpox as a way in which God clarified the colonists’ title to the land.

personas/john-mason/resumen.texto: English soldier, a veteran of the Dutch wars, who led the Connecticut forces in the Pequot War and burned the Mystic fort in May 1637. His account of the war, written around 1656, was published in 1736.

personas/john-underhill/resumen.texto: Massachusetts captain who took part in the attack on Mystic and justified it in “Newes from America” (1638). He later served the Dutch in Kieft’s War and in 1644 led the massacre of an Indigenous village near Pound Ridge.

personas/roger-williams/resumen.texto: Puritan minister banished from Massachusetts in 1635, among other reasons for holding that the king’s charter did not give a right to Indian land unless it was bought from them. He founded Providence on land ceded by the Narragansetts, defended the separation of church and state, and published “A Key into the Language of America” in 1643.

personas/john-eliot/resumen.texto: Puritan minister of Roxbury who learned the Massachusett language with Indigenous interpreters, preached in it from 1646, and from 1651 organized the “praying towns” of Christian Indians. With the Indigenous translators and printers John Sassamon, Job Nesutan and James Printer he published the complete Bible in Massachusett (1663), the first printed in the Americas, and a grammar (1666).

personas/caleb-cheeshahteaumuck/resumen.texto: Wampanoag from Martha’s Vineyard, the first Indigenous graduate of Harvard, in 1665. He died of tuberculosis the following year; a letter of his in Latin from 1663, addressed to English benefactors, survives.

personas/mary-rowlandson/resumen.texto: Wife of the minister of Lancaster (Massachusetts), captured in the February 1676 attack during King Philip’s War. She spent eleven weeks with Narragansetts, Nipmucs and Wampanoag until she was ransomed for twenty pounds; her narrative (1682) inaugurated the New England captivity literature.

personas/nathaniel-bacon/resumen.texto: Recently arrived landowner in Virginia who in 1676 led a rebellion of settlers against Governor Berkeley, demanding war against all Indigenous peoples; his men also attacked peoples allied with the colony. He burned Jamestown in September and died of dysentery in October 1676.

personas/william-penn/resumen.texto: English Quaker who in 1681 received the charter of Pennsylvania from Charles II in payment of a debt owed to his father. He bought the land occupied by the Lenape with deeds, and in 1681 wrote to them that he wished to enjoy that land with their love and consent and to live with them as neighbors and friends; in 1737 his sons used a dubious deed for the “Walking Purchase.”

personas/peter-minuit/resumen.texto: Director of New Netherland (1626–1631), to whom the purchase of Manhattan from the Lenape in 1626 is attributed. In 1638 he founded New Sweden in the service of Sweden, and he died that year in a hurricane in the Caribbean.

personas/willem-kieft/resumen.texto: Director of New Netherland who in 1639 sought to collect tribute from neighboring peoples and in February 1643 ordered the night attacks on Lenape refugees at Pavonia and Corlears Hook, with about 120 dead. The war that followed ruined the colony; he died in the shipwreck of the vessel that was carrying him to render an account.

personas/eleazar-wheelock/resumen.texto: Congregationalist minister from Connecticut who in 1754 opened the Moor's Charity School for young Indigenous people, among them Joseph Brant. With the money Samson Occom raised in Great Britain he founded Dartmouth College in 1769, where white students soon outnumbered Indigenous ones.

personas/samson-occom/resumen.texto: Mohegan from Connecticut, a student of Wheelock and a Presbyterian minister, who in 1766–1768 preached in Great Britain and raised some 12,000 pounds for the education of Indigenous people. He broke with Wheelock when the latter used that money for Dartmouth; in 1772 he published a widely circulated sermon, and in 1785 he founded the Indigenous Christian community of Brothertown, in New York.

personas/william-johnson/resumen.texto: Irishman who made a fortune as a trader in the Mohawk Valley, learned the language and was adopted by the Mohawk. As British superintendent of Indian affairs for the north (1756–1774) he conducted diplomacy with the Six Nations, made peace with Pontiac and negotiated the Treaty of Fort Stanwix (1768); he had eight children with the Mohawk woman Molly Brant.

personas/pontiac/resumen.texto: Odawa war leader of the Detroit region who in May 1763 laid siege to the British fort, in an uprising that bears his name although many peoples with leaders of their own took part. He made peace with William Johnson in 1766 and was assassinated in 1769 by a Peoria man in Cahokia.

personas/jeffery-amherst/resumen.texto: British commander in chief in North America, who took Louisbourg (1758) and Montreal (1760). After the war he cut the gifts and gunpowder given to Indigenous peoples, one of the causes of the 1763 rebellion, and during that war he proposed in a letter to Bouquet spreading smallpox among the rebels.

personas/henry-bouquet/resumen.texto: Swiss officer in British service who in August 1763 defeated Delawares, Shawnees and Mingos at Bushy Run and lifted the siege of Fort Pitt. In his July 1763 letters with Amherst he accepted the idea of spreading smallpox with blankets; in 1764 he forced the peoples of the Ohio to return hundreds of white captives.

personas/william-trent/resumen.texto: Pennsylvania fur trader and militia captain at Fort Pitt during the 1763 siege. His diary records that on June 24 two Delaware envoys were given two blankets and a handkerchief from the smallpox hospital, in the hope that they would have “the desired effect.”

personas/benjamin-franklin/resumen.texto: Printer, scientist and politician from Philadelphia, who printed the treaty minutes with the Iroquois and in a 1751 letter cited the union of the Six Nations as an example for the colonies. In 1764 he denounced the massacre of the Conestoga by the Paxton Boys; he signed the Declaration of Independence and negotiated the Treaty of Paris of 1783.

personas/logan-mingo/resumen.texto: Cayuga orator and war leader, son of Shikellamy, who settled in Ohio among the Mingo and until then had been a friend of the colonists. In 1774 Virginia settlers killed his family at Yellow Creek; he avenged them with raids and refused to make peace, with a message that Jefferson published in 1785. The exact text, its authorship and its accusation against Michael Cresap have been disputed ever since.

personas/joseph-brant/resumen.texto: Mohawk educated at Wheelock's school and protégé of William Johnson, who lived with his sister Molly Brant. He fought on the British side in the War of Independence, translated the Gospel of Mark into Mohawk and in 1784 led the loyalist Mohawk to lands on the Grand River, in present-day Ontario.

personas/george-washington/resumen.texto: Virginia planter and slaveholder whose 1754 clash with a French party began the French and Indian War. He commanded the Continental Army and in 1779 ordered the Sullivan Expedition against the Iroquois; in 1790 Seneca chiefs reminded him that this was why they called him “destroyer of villages.” As first president (1789–1797) he oversaw the Northwest War and the policy of “civilization” of Indigenous people.

personas/thomas-jefferson/resumen.texto: Virginia planter and slaveholder, drafter of the Declaration of Independence and third president (1801–1809). In “Notes on the State of Virginia” he defended the capacities of Indigenous Americans against Buffon and published Logan's speech; as president he bought Louisiana (1803) and proposed moving to the west of the Mississippi those peoples who did not accept agriculture and the cession of land.

personas/david-zeisberger/resumen.texto: Moravian missionary born in Moravia who worked for more than sixty years with the Lenape, wrote grammars and dictionaries of Lenape and Onondaga, and founded the Christian villages of Schoenbrunn and Gnadenhutten in Ohio (1772). In 1781 the British arrested him and moved his converts.

personas/little-turtle/resumen.texto: Miami war leader who, with the Shawnee Blue Jacket, defeated the armies of Harmar (1790) and St. Clair (1791). After Fallen Timbers he signed the Treaty of Greenville (1795) and from then on defended peace with the United States and the adoption of agriculture.

personas/tecumseh/resumen.texto: Shawnee leader who, with his brother Tenskwatawa, from 1808 gathered a confederation of peoples at Prophetstown to halt land cessions, on the idea that the land was common to all Indigenous peoples and that no people could sell it separately. He allied with the British in the War of 1812 and died at the Battle of the Thames in October 1813.

personas/tenskwatawa/resumen.texto: The Shawnee “Prophet,” brother of Tecumseh, who from 1805 preached the rejection of alcohol and of white customs and the persecution of Indigenous “sorcerers,” several of whom were executed by his followers. His prestige collapsed after the defeat at Tippecanoe (1811).

personas/sequoyah/resumen.texto: Cherokee silversmith who could not read in any language and who between 1809 and 1821 invented a syllabary of 86 characters (today 85) for Cherokee, which he made known in 1821 and which the nation officially adopted in 1825. He died in Mexico around 1843, while searching for Cherokees who had emigrated.

personas/john-ross-cherokee/resumen.texto: Principal chief of the Cherokee Nation from 1828 to 1866, of Scottish father and a mother from a mixed-race Cherokee family. He led his nation's legal defense before the Supreme Court and Congress, rejected the Treaty of New Echota and directed the last stage of the removal of 1838–1839.
