personas/andrew-jackson/resumen.texto: General and slaveholding planter from Tennessee who defeated the Creek “Red Sticks” at Horseshoe Bend (1814) and imposed the Treaty of Fort Jackson, which ceded some 9 million hectares, also from Creeks who had been his allies. As president (1829–1837) he promoted the Indian Removal Act of 1830 and did not enforce the ruling in Worcester v. Georgia.

personas/john-marshall/resumen.texto: Chief Justice of the United States Supreme Court from 1801 to 1835. His rulings of 1823, 1831 and 1832 established that Indigenous peoples were “domestic dependent nations” with a right of occupancy over their lands, which they could sell only to the federal government, and that they were outside the reach of state laws.

personas/peter-burnett/resumen.texto: First governor of the state of California (1849–1851). In his message to the legislature in January 1851 he said that the “war of extermination” between the races should be expected to continue until the extinction of the Indian race, and that preventing it was beyond the reach of government.

personas/vitus-bering/resumen.texto: Danish naval officer in the service of Russia who in 1728 crossed the strait that bears his name and in July 1741 sighted the coast of Alaska. On the return voyage he was shipwrecked on Bering Island, where he died of scurvy.

personas/georg-steller/resumen.texto: German naturalist on Bering's expedition, who landed on Kayak Island in July 1741 and for the first time described the flora and fauna of the Alaskan coast, including the sea cow that bears his name and was extinct a few decades later. His journal is the main source for the voyage.

personas/grigori-shelikhov/resumen.texto: Fur merchant from Rylsk who in 1784 founded the first permanent Russian settlement in America, on Kodiak Island. That year his men attacked the Alutiiq refugees at Awa'uq, and he took hostage the children of the island's families; his company became the basis of the Russian-American Company.

personas/alexander-baranov/resumen.texto: Merchant who managed Shelikhov's company in Alaska from 1790 and was the first manager of the Russian-American Company until 1818. He organized otter hunting with Aleut and Alutiiq hunters who were forced to serve in rotation, retook Sitka from the Tlingit in 1804, and under his direction Fort Ross was founded in California (1812).

hechos/viaje-de-ponce-de-leon-a-florida/.texto: Ponce de León Arrives in Florida

In 1513 Juan Ponce de León, former governor of Puerto Rico, set out under a royal capitulation to discover the island of “Bimini,” touched the Atlantic coast of the peninsula and named it Florida after the Pascua Florida; he explored the keys and the west coast, where the Calusa repulsed him. The story that he was seeking the “fountain of youth” appears in later chroniclers (Oviedo mentions it mockingly and Herrera asserts it in 1601), not in his capitulation. In 1521 he returned to settle, was wounded by the Calusa and died in Cuba.

hechos/colonia-de-san-miguel-de-gualdape.texto: The Colony of San Miguel de Gualdape
San Miguel de Gualdape (Georgia coast, uncertain site)

In 1526 Lucas Vázquez de Ayllón brought some 600 colonists, with enslaved Africans and Dominican friars — among them Antonio de Montesinos — to the coast of present-day South Carolina and Georgia, guided by an Indigenous man captured in 1521 whom they baptized Francisco de Chicora. They founded San Miguel de Gualdape, the first attempt at European settlement in the territory of the present-day continental United States; after Ayllón's death, hunger, disease, an uprising by the enslaved and conflicts with Indigenous peoples led some 150 survivors to abandon it after three months.

hechos/expedicion-de-narvaez/titulo.texto: The Narváez Expedition and Cabeza de Vaca's Journey

hechos/expedicion-de-narvaez/resumen.texto: About 600 men set out from Sanlúcar in 1527 to conquer Florida; they landed near Tampa Bay in April 1528 and marched to Apalachee, where they found no gold and were harassed by the Apalachee. They built rafts that were wrecked on the coast of Texas; of those who reached land, only four — Álvar Núñez Cabeza de Vaca, Andrés Dorantes, Alonso del Castillo and the enslaved man Estebanico — reached Culiacán in 1536, after living eight years among peoples of Texas and northern Mexico as enslaved people, traders and healers.

hechos/expedicion-de-hernando-de-soto/re.texto: About 600 men, with horses, pigs and war dogs, landed at Tampa Bay in May 1539 and for four years traveled through the Mississippian chiefdoms of the Southeast (Apalachee, Cofitachequi, Coosa, Tascalusa, Chicaza) as far as beyond the Mississippi. According to the four accounts of the expedition, they took maize, women and chained porters, mutilated people as punishment and set dogs on prisoners; de Soto died in 1542 and about 311 survivors reached Pánuco by boat in 1543. Archaeologists debate how much of the disappearance of the great Southeastern chiefdoms was due to this entrada and to the epidemics it may have left behind.

hechos/batalla-de-mabila/resumen.texto: On October 18, 1540, Tascalusa's warriors attacked de Soto's column inside the fortified town of Mabila, in present-day Alabama, and the Spaniards set the town on fire. The Gentleman of Elvas gives some 2,500 Indigenous dead, Rangel about 3,000 and Garcilaso more than 11,000, a figure considered greatly exaggerated; none can be verified, and the Spaniards lost some twenty men, many horses and almost all their baggage. The exact site has not been found.

hechos/viaje-de-fray-marcos-de-niza/titu.texto: Fray Marcos de Niza's Journey and the Death of Estebanico

hechos/viaje-de-fray-marcos-de-niza/resu.texto: Sent by Viceroy Antonio de Mendoza, Fray Marcos left Culiacán in March 1539 with Estebanico as guide and with Indigenous people from northern Mexico. Estebanico, who went ahead, was killed by the Zuni of Hawikuh; Fray Marcos said he had seen the city of Cíbola from afar, “greater than the city of Mexico,” and his account set off the Coronado expedition.

hechos/expedicion-de-coronado/resumen.texto: About 350 Spaniards, more than a thousand Indigenous allies from central Mexico, and African and Indigenous enslaved people set out from Compostela in February 1540. They took Hawikuh by storm in July, reached the Grand Canyon and the Hopi villages, wintered among the Tiwa of the Rio Grande and in 1541 followed an Indigenous guide, the “Turk,” to Quivira, in Kansas, where they found only Wichita villages; the Turk was executed. They returned in 1542 without riches, and the 1544 inquiry judged the expedition's abuses.

hechos/guerra-de-tiguex/lugar.texto: Tiguex (Tiwa pueblos of the Rio Grande)

hechos/guerra-de-tiguex/resumen.texto: In the winter of 1540–1541 Coronado's expedition demanded clothing and food from the Tiwa pueblos of the Rio Grande and evicted one of them to lodge there; the abuses, among them the rape of a woman, led the Tiwa to kill horses, and war broke out. At the village of Arenal the Spaniards burned about thirty prisoners who had surrendered, tied to stakes, and after the siege of Moho they killed many of those who were fleeing. García López de Cárdenas, who led the attack on Arenal, was prosecuted and convicted in Spain for these acts.

hechos/expedicion-de-tristan-de-luna/tit.texto: Tristán de Luna's Colony in Pensacola

hechos/expedicion-de-tristan-de-luna/res.texto: In August 1559 Tristán de Luna landed with some 1,500 people — soldiers, colonists, women, and African and Indigenous enslaved people from central Mexico — in Pensacola Bay to settle Florida. A hurricane sank most of the ships carrying provisions within a few weeks; the colony survived on maize taken from the inland peoples and was abandoned in 1561. Since 1992 remains of several of its ships have been found in the bay.

hechos/fuerte-carolina-y-matanzas/titulo.texto: Fort Caroline and the Executions at Matanzas

hechos/fuerte-carolina-y-matanzas/resume.texto: In 1564 French Huguenots led by Laudonnière built Fort Caroline on the St. Johns River, allied with the Timucua chief Saturiwa. Philip II sent Pedro Menéndez de Avilés, who in September 1565 took the fort and killed about 130 men; days later he had some 245 shipwreck survivors of Ribault's fleet who had surrendered beheaded in two groups at the Matanzas inlet, and he spared those who declared themselves Catholic. Menéndez justified the execution on the grounds that they were “Lutherans.” In 1568 the Frenchman Dominique de Gourgues, with Timucua allies, hanged the Spanish soldiers of the forts on the river.

hechos/fundacion-de-san-agustin-florida/.texto: Pedro Menéndez de Avilés founded St. Augustine on September 8, 1565, next to the Timucua village of Seloy, as a base against the French and to protect the route of the fleet from the Indies. It is the oldest continuously inhabited European-founded city in the continental United States; it was the capital of Spanish Florida until 1763 and again between 1784 and 1821.

hechos/mision-de-ajacan/resumen.texto: In 1570 eight Jesuits landed in Chesapeake Bay, guided by Paquiquineo, an Indigenous man baptized don Luis de Velasco, who had lived almost a decade in Spain, Mexico and Cuba. Don Luis returned to his people and in February 1571 the Jesuits were killed; only one boy survived, Alonso de Olmos. In 1572 Menéndez de Avilés hanged several Indigenous people in reprisal, and the Jesuits left Florida.

hechos/rebelion-de-guale/resumen.texto: In September 1597 a group of Guale from the Georgia coast, led according to Spanish documents by Juanillo, heir to a chiefdom whose friar had reprimanded him for keeping several wives, killed five Franciscans and burned missions. Governor Gonzalo Méndez de Canzo responded by burning villages and granaries; the Guale missions were rebuilt from 1605.

hechos/misiones-de-la-florida/resumen.texto: From 1587 the Franciscans founded missions among the Timucua, Guale and Apalachee; in 1655 they reported some 26,000 Christian Indians, and the villages had to send workers in rotation to St. Augustine (repartimiento) and carry goods. Fray Francisco Pareja published catechisms and a Timucua grammar in Mexico between 1612 and 1627, the first printed books in an Indigenous language of present-day United States. Epidemics, the Timucua rebellion of 1656 and the attacks by Carolina and its allies (1702–1706) destroyed the system.

hechos/fuerte-mose/titulo.texto: Gracia Real de Santa Teresa de Mose

hechos/fuerte-mose/lugar.texto: Gracia Real de Santa Teresa de Mose

hechos/fuerte-mose/resumen.texto: Fortified village north of St. Augustine where Governor Manuel de Montiano settled in 1738 enslaved Africans who had fled from Carolina, to whom a cédula of 1693 had offered freedom if they became Catholic. Under the command of the Mandinga Francisco Menéndez, it was the first legally recognized settlement of free Black people in what is now the United States; the Spanish offer was one of the causes of the Stono Rebellion (1739) in South Carolina.

hechos/colonizacion-de-nuevo-mexico/luga.texto: Ohkay Owingeh (San Juan de los Caballeros)

hechos/colonizacion-de-nuevo-mexico/resu.texto: In 1598 Juan de Oñate crossed the Rio Grande with about 130 soldiers and their families, Franciscans, enslaved people and thousands of head of livestock, took possession of New Mexico on April 30, and settled in the Tewa village of Ohkay Owingeh, which he named San Juan de los Caballeros. The entry was made under the Ordinances of 1573, which required speaking of “pacification” rather than “conquest” and attracting Indigenous people through good treatment; the peoples had to swear obedience to the king and hand over maize and blankets as tribute.

hechos/masacre-de-acoma/titulo.texto: The Taking of Acoma and the 1599 Trial

hechos/masacre-de-acoma/resumen.texto: In December 1598 the Acoma killed Juan de Zaldívar and about ten of his men, who had gone up onto their mesa to ask for provisions. In January 1599 Vicente de Zaldívar took the mesa after three days of fighting; some 800 Acoma died and some 500 were captured. At the trial in Santo Domingo, Oñate sentenced the men over 25 years old to amputation of one foot and twenty years of servitude, and the women and young people to twenty years of servitude; according to the record, the amputation was applied to 24 men, although some historians doubt that it was carried out in this way, and the sentence weighed in the 1614 trial against Oñate.

hechos/fundacion-de-santa-fe-nuevo-mexic.texto: Governor Pedro de Peralta moved New Mexico's capital around 1610 to the new town of Santa Fe, where the Palace of the Governors was built. During the 17th century the town was the center of conflicts between governors and Franciscans over control of the labor and tribute of the peoples.

hechos/rebelion-de-los-indios-pueblo/res.texto: On August 10, 1680, the Rio Grande peoples, who spoke different languages and were coordinated by Po'pay with cords of knots that marked the days, rose against the Spaniards after decades of tribute, forced labor, persecution of their ceremonies, drought and Apache attacks. They killed 21 of the 33 Franciscans and some 380 colonists, besieged Santa Fe and forced Governor Otermín to retreat with about 2,000 survivors, among them Indigenous allies, to El Paso. They destroyed churches and images, and the Spaniards did not return until 1692; it is usually considered the most successful Indigenous uprising against a European power in North America.

hechos/reconquista-de-nuevo-mexico/titul.texto: The Return of the Spaniards to New Mexico

hechos/reconquista-de-nuevo-mexico/resum.texto: In 1692 Diego de Vargas entered Santa Fe without combat, with promises of pardon; when he returned with colonists in December 1693 he took the town by storm, had some seventy defenders executed and distributed about four hundred women and children as servants. After another rebellion in 1696, the regime that followed was less harsh: the encomienda was not reestablished, and the Franciscans tolerated the ceremonies of the peoples more, which continued in the kivas.

hechos/genizaros/resumen.texto: Indigenous peoples of the plains and the Great Basin (Apaches, Comanches, Utes, Navajos, Paiutes) bought or “ransomed” from captivity by New Mexico colonists, raised as Christian servants and later freed but without a people of their own. They formed frontier villages such as Abiquiú (1754). The Laws of the Indies prohibited enslaving Indigenous people, but the authorities tolerated “ransom” as an act of charity that saved captives, and this trade with Comanches, Utes and other peoples continued in practice until after 1850.

hechos/misiones-de-texas/lugar.texto: Mission San Antonio de Valero (The Alamo)

hechos/misiones-de-texas/resumen.texto: Spain founded missions in East Texas from 1690, in response to La Salle's French colony, and in 1718 the Mission San Antonio de Valero and the Béxar presidio, origin of San Antonio. The missions drew mainly Coahuiltecan peoples seeking protection from Apaches and Comanches, but they had small populations and many desertions; they were secularized between 1793 and 1824.

hechos/destruccion-de-la-mision-de-san-s.texto: The Destruction of the San Sabá Mission
Mission Santa Cruz de San Sabá

In 1757 a mission was founded on the San Saba River for the Lipan Apaches, who never settled in it. In March 1758 some two thousand Comanches, Wichitas and allies, enemies of the Apaches and armed with French muskets, destroyed it and killed eight people, including two Franciscans; the punitive expedition of 1759 was turned back at the Red River.

hechos/paz-con-los-comanches-1786/titulo.texto: The 1786 Peace between New Mexico and the Comanches

hechos/paz-con-los-comanches-1786/resume.texto: After defeating the chief Cuerno Verde in 1779, Governor Juan Bautista de Anza agreed in February 1786, at Pecos, to peace with Ecueracapa, chosen by the Comanche bands as their representative: regulated trade, annual gifts and an alliance against the Apaches. The peace lasted until Mexican independence and is one of the best-documented agreements in the diplomacy of the northern frontier.

hechos/expedicion-de-portola/resumen.texto: On orders from the visitor José de Gálvez, who was worried by the Russian advance, two land columns and three ships left Baja California in 1769. They founded San Diego in July 1769 and, after passing Monterey Bay without recognizing it and discovering San Francisco Bay, founded Monterey in June 1770; scurvy killed most of the sailors. Among those who went were Gaspar de Portolá, Junípero Serra and the engineer Miguel Costansó.

hechos/misiones-de-california/lugar.texto: Mission San Carlos Borromeo de Carmelo

hechos/misiones-de-california/resumen.texto: The Franciscans founded 21 missions between San Diego (1769) and Sonoma (1823), protected by four presidios, and baptized some 80,000 Indigenous people. Those baptized could not leave without permission, and runaways were hunted down by soldiers; forced labor, flogging and the nightly confinement of young women were part of the system, and the missions' own records show that disease, infant mortality and low birthrates reduced the coastal peoples by half or more (Cook, 1943; Hackel, 2005). For their defenders, such as the Franciscan historian Francis Guest, they were institutions of evangelization and protection that taught agriculture and trades; for critics such as Cook or the Cahuilla Rupert Costo, they were a system of forced labor, and the canonization of Serra in 2015 revived the debate.

hechos/levantamiento-de-san-diego-1775/t.texto: The Kumeyaay Uprising at San Diego

hechos/levantamiento-de-san-diego-1775/r.texto: On the night of November 4–5, 1775, several hundred Kumeyaay from numerous villages attacked and set fire to the Mission San Diego, and they killed the Franciscan Luis Jayme and two Spanish artisans. Serra asked the viceroy that those responsible not be executed, so as not to thwart the conversion of the region; the mission was rebuilt.

hechos/rebelion-de-los-quechanes/resumen.texto: In July 1781 the Quechan (Yuma) of the Colorado River crossing, until then allies of the Spaniards and dissatisfied with the settlers occupying their lands and with the scarcity of gifts, destroyed the two mission-pueblos founded there in 1780 and 1781. They killed more than a hundred Spaniards, among them four Franciscans, such as Francisco Garcés, and Captain Fernando Rivera y Moncada, and took women and children captive; the overland route between Sonora and California was closed.

hechos/secularizacion-de-las-misiones-de.texto: The Secularization of the California Missions
Mission San Carlos Borromeo de Carmelo

The Mexican Congress ordered the secularization of the missions in 1833, and Governor José Figueroa applied it from 1834: part of the land and livestock was to be distributed among the neophytes. In practice most of it passed to Californio ranchos, and the former neophytes remained as peons on them or in the towns.

hechos/viajes-de-cartier/resumen.texto: In 1534 Cartier explored the Gulf of St. Lawrence, planted a cross at Gaspé and took two sons of the chief Donnacona. In 1535–1536 he went up the river to Stadacona and Hochelaga; in the winter 25 of his men died of scurvy, and the others were cured with an infusion of a tree that the Iroquois showed them. Before returning he seized Donnacona and nine others, who died in France; the attempt at a colony with Roberval in 1541–1543 failed, and the Iroquois of the St. Lawrence disappeared before 1600 for reasons that are debated.

hechos/fundacion-de-quebec/resumen.texto: Samuel de Champlain built a fortified “habitation” in July 1608 at the narrows of the St. Lawrence, on the site of the former Stadacona, as a base for the fur trade with the Montagnais and Algonquins; of the 28 men of the first winter, 8 survived. It was the capital of New France; it was in English hands from 1629 to 1632.

hechos/batalla-de-1609-contra-los-mohawk.texto: Champlain and the 1609 Battle against the Mohawk

On July 29, 1609, near present-day Ticonderoga, Champlain and two Frenchmen joined a party of Montagnais, Algonquins and Hurons against about two hundred Mohawk. According to his account, he killed two Mohawk chiefs with an arquebus shot and wounded a third; the battle sealed the French alliance with the peoples of the St. Lawrence and the enmity of the Iroquois League.

hechos/guerras-de-los-castores/resumen.texto: A cycle of wars in which the Iroquois League (Haudenosaunee), armed with Dutch and English muskets, attacked neighboring peoples, many of them French allies (Hurons, Petuns, Neutrals, Erie, Algonquins and others), and also the Susquehannocks, allies of the Dutch and Swedes. Historians debate whether the main motive was control of the furs or “mourning wars” to take captives who would replace the dead from epidemics. The Iroquois adopted many prisoners and tortured and killed others, and the Jesuits described cases of ritual cannibalism, a practice that the Hurons also had with their prisoners. The wars ended with the Great Peace of Montreal (1701).

hechos/epidemias-entre-los-hurones/resum.texto: Between 1634 and 1640 measles, influenza and smallpox epidemics reduced the Hurons from between 20,000 and 30,000 people to some 10,000, according to Trigger's estimates based on the Jesuit Relations. Many Hurons blamed the missionaries, who baptized the dying, and some councils discussed killing them.

hechos/mision-jesuita-entre-los-hurones/.texto: The Jesuit Mission among the Hurons

The Recollects from 1615 and the Jesuits from 1634 ministered among the Hurons, commercial allies of New France. The Jesuits learned the language, wrote grammars and dictionaries and from 1639 built the fortified base of Sainte-Marie; the mission divided the Hurons between Christians and traditionalists, and the Christians had better conditions for buying firearms from the French.

hechos/destruccion-de-huronia/resumen.texto: In 1648 and in March 1649 Mohawk and Seneca warriors destroyed the Huron villages of Saint-Joseph, Saint-Ignace and Saint-Louis, killed or captured hundreds of people, and put to death the Jesuits Antoine Daniel, Jean de Brébeuf and Gabriel Lalemant with ritual torture. The Jesuits burned Sainte-Marie and took refuge with a few thousand Hurons on Gahoendoe Island, where many died of hunger in the winter of 1649–1650. The survivors scattered: some were adopted by the Iroquois, others settled near Quebec (Wendake), and others, with the Petuns, formed the Wyandot people.

hechos/fundacion-del-hotel-dieu-de-quebe.texto: Founding of the Hôtel-Dieu de Quebec

Three Augustinian Hospitallers from Dieppe arrived in Quebec on August 1, 1639 with funds from the Duchess of Aiguillon, niece of Cardinal Richelieu, and founded the first hospital in New France. They first cared for Indigenous people sick with smallpox at the Sillery mission and then for colonists and Indigenous people in Quebec; the hospital still operates.

hechos/llegada-de-las-ursulinas-a-quebec.texto: On the same ship as the Hospitallers arrived Marie de l'Incarnation, two other Ursulines and the benefactress Madeleine de la Peltrie, who opened the first girls' school in New France. They received Huron, Algonquin and Iroquois students as well as French ones, with the aim of educating them in the French manner, and Marie de l'Incarnation acknowledged in her letters that very few adapted to that life.

hechos/fundacion-de-montreal/resumen.texto: The Society of Notre-Dame de Montréal, an association of French devotees, founded Ville-Marie in May 1642, with Paul de Chomedey de Maisonneuve and Jeanne Mance, as a mission to convert Indigenous people. Jeanne Mance opened the Hôtel-Dieu there; harassed by the Iroquois for decades, the town became the center of the fur trade.

hechos/fundacion-del-seminario-de-quebec.texto: Founding of the Seminary of Quebec

Bishop François de Laval founded the Seminary of Quebec in 1663 to train priests, and in 1668 a minor seminary that also admitted some Huron boys, who soon left. It is the origin of Laval University (1852).

hechos/viaje-de-marquette-y-jolliet/titu.texto: Marquette and Jolliet on the Mississippi

hechos/viaje-de-marquette-y-jolliet/resu.texto: In May 1673 the Jesuit Jacques Marquette and the trader Louis Jolliet left Michilimackinac with five oarsmen, followed the Fox and Wisconsin rivers to the Mississippi and went down it to the mouth of the Arkansas, among the Quapaw, where they became convinced that the river flowed into the Gulf of Mexico. They returned by the Illinois River; their voyage opened the way to Louisiana.

hechos/la-salle-y-la-luisiana/resumen.texto: In April 1682 La Salle reached the mouth of the Mississippi and took possession of its entire basin for Louis XIV, naming it Louisiana. In 1685 he returned by sea with some 300 colonists, did not find the river, and landed in Matagorda Bay, Texas, where he founded Fort Saint-Louis. La Salle was murdered by his men in 1687, and the Karankawas destroyed the fort around 1689. The Spanish alarm led to the founding of missions in Texas.

hechos/gran-paz-de-montreal/resumen.texto: In August 1701 Governor Louis-Hector de Callière and some 1,300 representatives of about forty Indigenous nations, from the Iroquois League to the Great Lakes allies, signed a general peace, marked with the marks of their clans. It ended nearly a century of Beaver Wars; the Iroquois committed to neutrality between the French and the English. The Wendat chief Kondiaronk, one of its architects, died during the conferences.

hechos/esclavitud-en-nueva-francia/resum.texto: The French bought war captives from their allies, from distant peoples generally called “panis,” and from the late 17th century also enslaved Africans; an ordinance of Intendant Raudot (1709) declared that both belonged as slaves to those who had bought them. According to the count of the historian Marcel Trudel, there were some 4,000 enslaved people in New France between 1632 and 1760, about two-thirds of them Indigenous.

hechos/fundacion-de-nueva-orleans/resume.texto: Bienville founded New Orleans in 1718 for John Law's Mississippi Company; from 1722 it was the capital of French Louisiana. From 1719 the company brought some 6,000 enslaved Africans, and the Code Noir of Louisiana (1724) regulated slavery. France ceded the city and western Louisiana to Spain in 1762; it returned to France in 1800, and Napoleon sold it to the United States in 1803.

hechos/rebelion-de-los-natchez/resumen.texto: The Natchez, the last chiefdom of Mississippian tradition, with a supreme chief called the Great Sun, a class society and human sacrifices at the funerals of the nobility, lived alongside the French fort of Rosalie. When the commandant wanted to take one of their villages, on November 28, 1729, they killed some 230 colonists and took women and enslaved Africans captive. The French and their Choctaw allies defeated them in 1730–1731: hundreds of Natchez, including the Great Sun, were sold as slaves in Saint-Domingue, and the survivors took refuge among the Chickasaws and the Creeks.

hechos/guerras-de-los-zorros/resumen.texto: The Meskwaki of Wisconsin, enemies of several Indigenous allies of France and of the passage of French traders toward the Sioux, fought for two decades against the French and their allies. In 1730 a Meskwaki column attempting to emigrate was besieged in Illinois, and some five hundred men, women and children were killed or enslaved; the government of New France then set out to destroy the people, and the survivors joined the Sauk.

hechos/deportacion-de-los-acadianos/resu.texto: During the French and Indian War, British authorities in Nova Scotia deported some 11,500 Acadians, French Catholic settlers who refused to swear unconditional loyalty to the Crown, and burned their villages. Thousands died on the ships and at their destinations, and many ended up in Louisiana, where they are the origin of the Cajuns. From 1749 both sides paid for scalps: the British governor Edward Cornwallis offered rewards for those of the Mi'kmaq, allies of the Acadians, and the French missionary Jean-Louis Le Loutre paid the Mi'kmaq for British scalps.

hechos/toma-de-quebec-1759/resumen.texto: On September 13, 1759, the British army of James Wolfe defeated Montcalm's army on the Plains of Abraham, near Quebec, and both generals died. The city surrendered days later, and the capitulation of Montreal (1760) left Canada in British hands; one of its articles guaranteed the Indigenous allies of France possession of the lands they inhabited.

hechos/colonia-de-roanoke/resumen.texto: Walter Raleigh sent a military colony in 1585 to Roanoke Island, in the land of the Algonquians of Carolina; after burning a village over the disappearance of a silver cup and killing the chief Wingina in 1586, the colonists returned to England. Thomas Harriot and John White studied the peoples of the area. The 1587 colony, with some 115 men, women and children, disappeared: in 1590 White found only the word “CROATOAN,” the name of an island of friendly Indigenous people, and its fate remains unresolved.

hechos/fundacion-de-jamestown/resumen.texto: In May 1607 some 104 colonists of the Virginia Company settled on a marshy peninsula in the James River, within the territory of the Powhatan Confederacy. Hunger and disease decimated them: in the winter of 1609–1610 the population fell from some 500 to about 60, and remains of a girl found in 2012 show she was dismembered after death, probably to be eaten, as the chronicles of that winter recount. Tobacco, cultivated from 1612, made the colony viable; in 1619 its assembly met and the first enslaved Africans arrived.

hechos/guerras-anglo-powhatan/resumen.texto: Three wars pitted Virginia against the Powhatan Confederacy. In the first (1609–1614) the English attacked villages, and at Paspahegh they killed the chief's wife and children; it ended with the marriage of Pocahontas. The second began with the 1622 attack and continued with English campaigns of crop burning and, in 1623, the poisoning of some two hundred Indigenous people at a peace negotiation on the Potomac; the third (1644–1646) ended with the death of Opechancanough and a treaty that left the Powhatan as tributaries of the colony.

hechos/ataque-powhatan-de-1622/resumen.texto: On March 22, 1622, Powhatan Confederacy warriors, led by Opechancanough, simultaneously attacked the scattered plantations along the James River and killed 347 colonists, about a quarter of the population. The Virginia Company and Smith presented it as a betrayal that justified a war without quarter and the seizure of Indigenous lands; for the Powhatan it was a response to the expansion of tobacco onto their lands and to the murder of the warrior Nemattanew.

hechos/epidemia-de-nueva-inglaterra-1616.texto: An epidemic of unknown cause killed much of the coastal population of New England between 1616 and 1619, from Maine to Cape Cod; the Plymouth colonists settled in 1620 at Patuxet, a depopulated village where they saw unburied bones. Smallpox, plague, hepatitis and leptospirosis have been proposed as causes (Marr and Cathey, 2010); mortality estimates range from a third to nine out of ten inhabitants, depending on the area and the author.

hechos/fundacion-de-plymouth/titulo.texto: The Plymouth Colony and the Alliance with Massasoit

hechos/fundacion-de-plymouth/resumen.texto: The 102 passengers of the Mayflower, about forty of them Separatist Puritans, arrived in November 1620 and settled at Patuxet; half of them died the first winter. In March 1621 Massasoit, sachem of the Wampanoag, signed a mutual-aid pact with them, with Squanto as interpreter; the colony was absorbed by Massachusetts in 1691.

hechos/cosecha-de-plymouth-1621/titulo.texto: The 1621 Harvest and the Myth of the “First Thanksgiving”

hechos/cosecha-de-plymouth-1621/resumen.texto: The only contemporary description is a letter by Edward Winslow published in 1622: after the harvest, the colonists held a celebration of several days, attended by Massasoit and about ninety men, who contributed five deer. Winslow does not call it a Thanksgiving; the idea of a founding “first Thanksgiving” arose in 1841, when an editor of that letter so named it, and it was established with the national holiday of 1863. Both the idyllic version of Pilgrims and Indians sharing the table and the version that confuses it with the massacre of 1637 mix up distinct events.

hechos/colonia-de-la-bahia-de-massachuse.texto: In 1630 about a thousand Puritans on eleven ships, with John Winthrop as governor, founded Boston and other towns; by about 1640 the “Great Migration” had brought some 20,000 colonists to New England. The colony's seal showed an Indigenous man saying “Come over and help us,” taken from the Acts of the Apostles, but the mission among Indigenous people only began in 1646.

hechos/viruela-de-1633-en-nueva-inglater.texto: The Smallpox Epidemic of 1633–1634 in New England

A smallpox epidemic killed much of the Massachusett, Pawtucket and peoples of the Connecticut Valley; Bradford describes villages where the sick had no one to bring them water or firewood, and the aid that some colonists gave. In 1634 Winthrop wrote that the Indigenous people had almost all died of smallpox and that thus the Lord had cleared the colonists' title to what they possessed.

hechos/guerra-pequot/resumen.texto: After the killing of two English traders, attributed to the Pequots or neighboring peoples, Massachusetts and Connecticut, with Mohegan and Narragansett allies, made war on the Pequots, who competed with all of them for the wampum trade of the Connecticut Valley. After the Mystic massacre the survivors were hunted down; many were killed and others were distributed as servants among colonists and allies or sold as slaves in Bermuda and on Providence Island in the Caribbean. The Treaty of Hartford (1638) declared the Pequot nation dissolved and forbade the use of its name.

hechos/matanza-de-mystic/resumen.texto: At dawn on May 26, 1637, some ninety colonists from Connecticut and Massachusetts under John Mason and John Underhill, with Mohegan and Narragansett allies, surrounded the Pequot fort at Mystic and set it on fire, and they killed those who escaped the flames. Between 400 and 700 Pequots died, mostly women, children and the elderly, because most of the warriors were at another fort. Mason and Bradford attributed it to the hand of God, and Underhill justified it with the Bible; according to Underhill, the allied Narragansetts protested that this form of war “kills too many men.”

hechos/compra-de-manhattan/resumen.texto: A letter from the official Pieter Schaghen to the States General, dated November 5, 1626, reports that the colonists “bought the island of Manhattan from the savages for the value of 60 guilders.” That is all that is known: no deed survives, the figure of “24 dollars” is a 19th-century conversion, and historians point out that the Lenape probably understood the agreement as permission for shared use and not as a sale.

hechos/guerra-de-kieft/resumen.texto: War between New Netherland and the Lenape and other Algonquian-speaking peoples of the Manhattan region. It began with the night attacks of February 1643 at Pavonia and Corlears Hook, ordered by Director Willem Kieft against Indigenous refugees; in 1644 colonial troops under John Underhill killed between 500 and 700 people in a village near Pound Ridge. More than a thousand Indigenous people died, the colony was ruined, and the colonists demanded the dismissal of Kieft.

hechos/nueva-suecia/resumen.texto: Swedish colony on the banks of the Delaware River, founded in 1638 by Peter Minuit at Fort Christina, which traded furs with the Lenape and the Susquehannocks and never exceeded a few hundred colonists, many of them Finns. Its pastor Johannes Campanius translated Luther's catechism into the Lenape language, printed in 1696. The Dutch under Peter Stuyvesant occupied it in 1655.

hechos/pueblos-de-oracion/resumen.texto: Communities of Christian Indigenous people organized by John Eliot in Massachusetts from Natick (1651), with self-government, schools and laws that banned Indigenous customs such as long hair on men. In 1674 there were fourteen, with about 1,100 people. During King Philip's War, under suspicion from the colonists, many of their inhabitants were interned on Deer Island, in Boston harbor, where many died of hunger and cold.

hechos/imprenta-de-cambridge/resumen.texto: The first printing press in the English colonies began operating in Cambridge, Massachusetts, in 1639, a century after the one in Mexico; its first surviving book is the Bay Psalm Book (1640). With funds from the Society for the Propagation of the Gospel, it printed from 1654 catechisms, primers and the Bible in Massachusett, with the participation of the Nipmuc printer James Printer.

hechos/colegio-indio-de-harvard/resumen.texto: Brick building erected at Harvard around 1655 with funds from the Society for the Propagation of the Gospel, since the college's 1650 charter included among its aims the education of “English and Indian” youth. Few Indigenous students used it — only Caleb Cheeshahteaumuck graduated, in 1665 — and it housed the printing press where Eliot's Bible was made; it was demolished around 1698.

hechos/guerra-del-rey-felipe/resumen.texto: War between the New England colonies, with Mohegan, Pequot and other Indigenous allies, and a coalition of Wampanoag, Narragansett, Nipmuc and other peoples led by Metacom. Indigenous forces attacked more than half of the colonists' towns and destroyed twelve of them; between 600 and 800 colonists and several thousand Indigenous people died in combat, from hunger or from disease. After the war hundreds of prisoners, including many who had surrendered, were sold as slaves to the Antilles and other destinations; relative to population, it is generally considered the deadliest war in the English colonies.

hechos/batalla-del-gran-pantano/titulo.texto: The Battle of the Great Swamp

hechos/batalla-del-gran-pantano/resumen.texto: On December 19, 1675, about a thousand militiamen from the United Colonies attacked the Narragansetts' winter fort in a swamp in Rhode Island, where the Narragansetts had until then been neutral, and set it on fire with its occupants inside. About seventy colonists and several hundred Narragansetts, many of them women and children, died; source figures range from about three hundred to a thousand.

hechos/rebelion-de-bacon/resumen.texto: Colonists on the Virginia frontier, who rejected Governor William Berkeley's policy of distinguishing between allied and enemy Indigenous peoples and of protecting the fur trade, followed Nathaniel Bacon in attacks on the Susquehannocks, Occaneechees and the Pamunkey, allies of the colony. Bacon burned Jamestown in September 1676, died in October, and the rebellion came apart; the Treaty of Middle Plantation (1677) recognized reservations for the tributary peoples.

hechos/penn-y-los-lenape/titulo.texto: Penn and the Lenape: The “Great Treaty”

hechos/penn-y-los-lenape/resumen.texto: William Penn bought the land of Pennsylvania from the Lenape with deeds signed from July 1682, paid for with goods, and the colony kept the peace with them for half a century. According to tradition, in 1682 he signed with the chief Tamanend a treaty of friendship under an elm at Shackamaxon, but no document of that agreement survives: the image comes from Voltaire, who praised it as the only treaty “never sworn and never broken,” and from Benjamin West's painting (1771–1772).

hechos/compra-de-la-caminata/resumen.texto: Thomas and John Penn presented the Lenape with a deed of 1686, of doubtful authenticity, that ceded the land a man could walk over in a day and a half. In September 1737 they hired trained runners who, along a road cleared in advance, covered more than a hundred kilometers, and they kept some 490,000 hectares of the Delaware Valley. When the Lenape protested, the colony asked the Iroquois League to force them to leave (1742).

hechos/trata-de-esclavos-indigenas-de-ca.texto: The Indigenous Slave Trade of Carolina

Charleston merchants paid the Westos, Savannas, Yamasees, Creeks, Chickasaws and other peoples with weapons and goods to capture Indigenous people from enemy peoples or from the Spanish missions, who were sold as slaves in the Antilles, New England and the plantations of Carolina. Gallay (2002) estimates that between 1670 and 1715 between 24,000 and 51,000 Indigenous people of the Southeast were sold. The slave raids, together with epidemics, reshaped the map of the region's peoples.

hechos/destruccion-de-las-misiones-de-ap.texto: The Destruction of the Apalachee Missions

In January 1704 former Carolina governor James Moore, with about fifty colonists and a thousand Creek warriors, attacked the Apalachee missions; according to Spanish testimony, they killed hundreds of Christian Indians, tortured and burned prisoners, among them a Franciscan, and carried off several thousand Apalachees: some as slaves, and others who, dissatisfied with life in the missions, left with them of their own accord. San Luis was abandoned in July 1704; by 1706 the Florida missions, except those near St. Augustine, had disappeared.

hechos/guerra-tuscarora/resumen.texto: In September 1711 the southern Tuscaroras and neighboring peoples attacked the North Carolina settlements, which were encroaching on their lands and seizing their people for the slave trade, and killed more than 130 colonists. South Carolina sent two expeditions with Yamasees and other allies; in March 1713 the capture of Fort Neoheroka left some 950 Tuscaroras dead or captured, and the captives were sold as slaves. Most Tuscaroras migrated north and joined the Iroquois League as its sixth nation around 1722.

hechos/guerra-yamasee/resumen.texto: In April 1715 the Yamasees, indebted to the Charleston merchants, who collected their debts by enslaving their families, killed Carolina's agents at Pocotaligo; Creeks, Catawbas and other peoples joined them. About 400 colonists died, some 7% of South Carolina's white population, along with most of the merchants who lived among the Indigenous peoples. Carolina's alliance with the Cherokees saved it; the war ended the great Indigenous slave trade of the Southeast, and the Yamasees took refuge near St. Augustine.

hechos/guerra-franco-india/resumen.texto: The North American branch of the Seven Years' War, which began in 1754 in the Ohio Valley with the clash of George Washington's Virginia militia with a French party. The French, with far fewer colonists, relied on their Indigenous allies, who defeated Braddock in 1755 and attacked the Pennsylvania and Virginia frontiers; Great Britain won with the capture of Louisbourg, Quebec and Montreal. By the Treaty of Paris of 1763 France ceded Canada and eastern Louisiana to Great Britain, after having ceded western Louisiana to Spain in 1762, without consulting the peoples who lived there.

hechos/rendicion-de-fort-william-henry/t.texto: The Surrender of Fort William Henry

hechos/rendicion-de-fort-william-henry/r.texto: In August 1757 the British garrison of the fort, on Lake George, surrendered to Montcalm with the promise that it could leave with honors. Indigenous warriors allied with the French, who expected plunder and captives, attacked the column: they killed between 69 and 184 people, according to the estimate of the historian Ian Steele, and took hundreds of captives. Cooper's novel “The Last of the Mohicans” (1826) inflated the figure; the warriors carried to their villages the smallpox that had been in the fort.

hechos/rebelion-de-pontiac/resumen.texto: In May 1763 Odawas, Ojibwes, Potawatomis, Hurons, Delawares, Shawnees, Senecas and other peoples of the Great Lakes and the Ohio attacked the forts the British had occupied after the French defeat: they took eight, besieged Detroit and Fort Pitt, and killed or captured hundreds of frontier colonists. They were driven by Amherst's policy of cutting gifts and gunpowder, the advance of the colonists, and the preaching of the Delaware prophet Neolin, who called for rejecting the whites and their goods. It ended with treaties in 1764–1766; Great Britain returned to the diplomacy of gifts and issued the Proclamation of 1763.

hechos/mantas-de-fort-pitt/resumen.texto: During the siege of Fort Pitt, on June 24, 1763, the fort's officers gave two Delaware envoys two blankets and a handkerchief from the smallpox hospital, according to William Trent's diary and the invoice the army paid. In July, separately, Amherst proposed in a letter to Bouquet spreading smallpox among the rebels, and Bouquet accepted the idea; there is no proof that this plan was carried out. There was smallpox among the peoples of the Ohio in 1763–1764, but it was already circulating in the region, and historians debate whether the blankets caused it (Fenn, 2000, considers it possible; Ranlet, 2000, doubts it). Versions in which blankets were distributed en masse or a general policy of biological warfare against Indigenous peoples was pursued have no documentary support.

hechos/matanza-de-los-conestoga/titulo.texto: The Conestoga Massacre by the Paxton Boys

hechos/matanza-de-los-conestoga/resumen.texto: In December 1763 Pennsylvania frontier militiamen, the “Paxton Boys,” killed six Conestogas in their village and then the fourteen remaining, whom the authorities had housed for their protection in the Lancaster workhouse. Many Conestogas were Christians, and all had lived in peace under the colony's protection; the attackers accused them of helping Pontiac's rebels. In February 1764 some 250 men marched on Philadelphia to kill the Moravian Indigenous refugees there, and Franklin negotiated their withdrawal; no one was tried.

hechos/tratado-de-fort-stanwix/resumen.texto: William Johnson gathered some 3,000 Iroquois and other Indigenous people at Fort Stanwix to push the Proclamation Line westward: the Six Nations ceded, in exchange for goods worth about 10,000 pounds, lands south of the Ohio River that were hunting grounds of the Shawnees, Delawares and Cherokees, who did not sign. The Shawnees rejected it, one of the causes of Dunmore's War (1774).

hechos/guerra-de-dunmore/titulo.texto: Lord Dunmore's War and Logan's Message

hechos/guerra-de-dunmore/resumen.texto: In April 1774 Virginia settlers killed relatives of the Mingo chief Logan at Yellow Creek, and he responded with raids. Governor Dunmore led the Virginia militia against the Shawnees, who were defeated at Point Pleasant in October and ceded their hunting grounds south of the Ohio at Camp Charlotte. Logan did not come to make peace and sent a message that Jefferson published in 1785 as an example of Indigenous eloquence: “Who is there to mourn for Logan? Not one.”

hechos/fundacion-de-dartmouth/resumen.texto: In 1769 Eleazar Wheelock obtained a royal charter to found a college in New Hampshire for the education of “the youth of the Indian tribes of this land,” as well as English youth, with the money Samson Occom had raised in Great Britain to educate Indigenous people. For two centuries very few Indigenous people graduated there; in 1970 the college took up that founding purpose again with a Native studies program.

hechos/escuela-india-de-william-and-mary.texto: The Indian School of William and Mary

The College of William and Mary, founded in 1693, received part of the bequest of the scientist Robert Boyle to educate Indigenous children, and in 1723 it built the Brafferton for them. Few students attended; some came as hostages for the good conduct of their peoples, and the school closed with the Revolution, when its English revenues were lost.

hechos/misiones-moravas/titulo.texto: The Moravian Missions among the Lenape

hechos/misiones-moravas/resumen.texto: The Moravian Brethren, a Pietist Protestant church of Czech origin based in Herrnhut (Saxony), missionized from 1740 among the Mahicans and Lenape of New York and Pennsylvania and later in Ohio, with David Zeisberger and John Heckewelder. They founded pacifist Christian villages, learned the languages and left journals that are a main source on the Lenape of the 18th century; their converts were suspected by both sides in every war.

hechos/pueblos-indigenas-en-la-guerra-de.texto: Indigenous Peoples in the War of Independence

Most of the peoples who took part supported the British, who had checked the advance of the colonists with the Proclamation of 1763; others, such as the Oneidas and Tuscaroras, the Catawbas and the Stockbridge Mohicans, fought with the rebels. The war divided the Iroquois League, whose members fought each other at Oriskany (1777), and on the frontier both sides attacked villages and farms. The Declaration of Independence accused the king of having incited the “merciless Indian savages” against the colonists.

hechos/campana-de-sullivan/titulo.texto: The Sullivan Campaign against the Iroquois

hechos/campana-de-sullivan/resumen.texto: On George Washington's orders, some 4,000 soldiers under John Sullivan and James Clinton traversed Seneca and Cayuga territory between June and October 1779 and destroyed more than forty villages, along with their cornfields and orchards, in retaliation for Iroquois and Loyalist attacks on the frontier. There were few combat casualties, but thousands of Iroquois spent the winter of 1779–1780 as refugees near the British fort of Niagara, short of food and suffering from disease.

hechos/matanza-de-gnadenhutten/resumen.texto: In early March 1782 Pennsylvania militiamen under David Williamson, who were looking for the perpetrators of frontier raids, detained Moravian Christian Lenape at Gnadenhutten (Ohio) who had returned to harvest their corn. After voting on their fate, on March 8 they beat 96 people to death, among them about 39 children. No one was tried; months later, in retaliation, the Lenape burned Colonel William Crawford alive.

hechos/independencia-de-estados-unidos/t.texto: The Independence of the United States

hechos/independencia-de-estados-unidos/r.texto: The Thirteen Colonies declared their independence on July 4, 1776, in Philadelphia and won it in the war against Great Britain (1775–1783), with French help from 1778 and Spanish help from 1779. The Treaty of Paris of 1783 recognized the United States, the first independent state in the Americas, with boundaries reaching the Mississippi, over lands that were for the most part Indigenous peoples' lands, whose peoples did not take part in the negotiation; the Constitution of 1787 gave Congress the power to regulate commerce “with the Indian tribes.”

hechos/guerra-del-noroeste/resumen.texto: The United States claimed the lands north of the Ohio as won from Great Britain and organized their sale, but a confederation of Shawnees, Miamis, Delawares, Wyandots and other peoples, backed by the British, defended the river as the border. It defeated Harmar in 1790 and, on November 4, 1791, the army of Arthur St. Clair, which suffered more than 600 dead, the worst defeat of an American army at the hands of Indigenous people. Anthony Wayne defeated the confederation at Fallen Timbers (1794), and the Treaty of Greenville (1795) ceded most of Ohio.

hechos/expedicion-de-bering-a-alaska/res.texto: As part of the Great Northern Expedition, the ships St. Peter, under Vitus Bering, and St. Paul, under Alekséi Chírikov, left Petropavlovsk in June 1741 and sighted the coast of Alaska in July; Chírikov lost two boats with fifteen men who never returned. On the return voyage the St. Peter was shipwrecked on Bering Island, where Bering and about thirty of its 77 men died; the survivors returned in 1742 with sea otter furs, which set off the fur rush.

hechos/cazadores-rusos-en-las-aleutianas.texto: From 1745 Siberian fur hunters (promyshlenniki) arrived in the Aleutians; they took hostages and forced Aleut men (Unangan) to hunt sea otters as tribute. The Aleuts resisted, especially in 1763–1764, when they destroyed four Russian ships in the Fox Islands, and the reprisals of Ivan Solovyov were very violent. Between the violence, epidemics and forced labor, the Aleut population fell from some 12,000 to 15,000 people to about 2,500 at the beginning of the 19th century, according to disputed estimates.

hechos/matanza-de-awa-uq/resumen.texto: In August 1784 the men of Grigori Shelikhov, newly landed on Kodiak Island, attacked Awa'uq, a rock refuge where Alutiiq (Sugpiaq) families had gathered. Death tolls range from about two hundred to several thousand depending on the source, between Alutiiq accounts and later Russian testimony. Shelikhov took the children of the island's families hostage to ensure their obedience, and he did not mention the attack in his published account.

hechos/compania-ruso-americana/resumen.texto: In 1799 Tsar Paul I gave Shelikhov's successor company the monopoly on trade and government in Russian America. Under Alexandr Baránov it employed Aleut and Alutiiq hunters, who were forced to serve in rotation, in expeditions that reached California; the Orthodox Church, with missionaries such as Ivan Veniaminov, who created a writing system for Aleut, baptized much of the coastal population.

hechos/batallas-de-sitka/resumen.texto: In June 1802 the Tlingit destroyed the Russian fort of St. Michael the Archangel, built in 1799 in their territory, and killed most of its Russian and Aleut occupants. In 1804 Baránov returned with a warship and hundreds of Aleut hunters; after several days of siege, the Tlingit abandoned their fort at night, and the Russians founded New Archangel, the capital of Russian America.

hechos/venta-de-alaska/resumen.texto: Russia sold Alaska to the United States for 7.2 million dollars in a treaty of March 30, 1867; the transfer took place at Sitka on October 18. No Indigenous people were consulted; the treaty distinguished the inhabitants who could become citizens from the “uncivilized tribes,” which would be subject to the laws the United States enacted.

hechos/confederacion-de-tecumseh/resumen.texto: From 1805 the Shawnee prophet Tenskwatawa and his brother Tecumseh gathered warriors from many peoples against land cessions, such as the one in the Treaty of Fort Wayne (1809). On November 7, 1811, in Tecumseh's absence, Governor William Henry Harrison defeated the Prophet's followers at Tippecanoe and burned Prophetstown. Tecumseh allied with the British in the War of 1812, and his death in 1813 ended the last attempt at a great Indigenous confederacy east of the Mississippi.

hechos/silabario-cherokee/resumen.texto: Sequoyah, who could not read in any language, completed around 1821 a system of 86 signs (now 85), one for each syllable, for writing Cherokee, which the nation officially adopted in 1825. Within a few years a large part of the Cherokees had learned to read and write in their language; from 1828 the newspaper Cherokee Phoenix was printed in it. It is one of the few documented cases of a writing system created by a person who could not read.

hechos/ley-de-traslado-de-1830/resumen.texto: On May 28, 1830, Andrew Jackson signed the law authorizing him to exchange the lands of the eastern peoples for lands west of the Mississippi; it was passed by a narrow margin in the House of Representatives, with opposition from evangelicals and part of Congress. The law spoke of voluntary removals, but the treaties were signed under pressure, with unrepresentative leaders or by force; until 1850 about 60,000 Choctaws, Creeks, Chickasaws, Cherokees and Seminoles were removed, along with thousands of people from the northern peoples, and thousands died on the way.

hechos/fallos-cherokees/titulo.texto: The Supreme Court Rulings on the Cherokees

hechos/fallos-cherokees/resumen.texto: In Cherokee Nation v. Georgia (1831) the Supreme Court declared that it lacked jurisdiction over the Cherokees’ suit and defined them as a “domestic dependent nation”; in Worcester v. Georgia (1832) it overturned the conviction of a missionary by Georgia and held that the state’s laws had no force in Cherokee territory. Georgia did not comply with the second ruling, and President Jackson did not enforce it; both remain the basis of Indigenous law in the United States.

hechos/tratado-de-new-echota/resumen.texto: In December 1835 a minority group of Cherokees, the “treaty party” of Major Ridge, John Ridge and Elias Boudinot, signed the cession of all eastern Cherokee lands in exchange for $5 million and lands in present-day Oklahoma. The nation’s council and Chief John Ross rejected it with a petition of some 15,000 signatures, but the Senate ratified it in 1836 with the bare votes needed for a two-thirds majority (31 to 15). In 1839 the three leaders were killed by supporters of Ross, who invoked the Cherokee law that punished the sale of the nation’s lands with death; Ross denied having known of it.

hechos/sendero-de-lagrimas/resumen.texto: After the deadline set by the New Echota treaty expired, the army and militias gathered some 16,000 Cherokees into detention camps in May 1838 and moved them overland and by river to Indian Territory (Oklahoma). About 4,000 died in the camps and on the way, according to the most widely cited estimate, from disease, cold and hunger; other estimates range from about 2,000 to about 8,000. The name is also applied to the removals of Choctaws, Creeks, Chickasaws and Seminoles in those years.

hechos/matanzas-de-california/resumen.texto: California’s Indigenous population fell from about 150,000 in 1848 to about 30,000 in 1870, according to Cook’s estimates, due to massacres by militias and civilians, disease, hunger and forced labor. The state financed volunteer militia campaigns, whose costs the federal government reimbursed, and the 1850 law allowed “vagrant” Indigenous people and minors to be taken as forced laborers; Governor Burnett spoke in 1851 of a “war of extermination.” Madley (2016) documents between about 9,500 and 16,000 deaths from homicide—part of the total decline, in which disease and hunger weighed more—and argues that the whole amounted to genocide under the 1948 convention; other historians, such as Gary Clayton Anderson, dispute the intent and prefer to speak of ethnic cleansing. In 2019 Governor Gavin Newsom apologized on behalf of the state and called it genocide.

hechos/matanza-de-bloody-island/resumen.texto: In December 1849 Pomo people working in servitude for Andrew Kelsey and Charles Stone by Clear Lake killed them after months of hunger and mistreatment. In May 1850 soldiers of the United States Army under Captain Nathaniel Lyon attacked an island in the lake where Pomo people who had not taken part had gathered, and killed between about sixty and several hundred, depending on the sources, mostly women and children.

hechos/matanza-de-sand-creek/resumen.texto: On November 29, 1864, some 675 Colorado volunteer soldiers under Colonel John Chivington attacked the camp of Cheyennes and Arapahos led by Chief Black Kettle, who considered himself at peace under the protection of the army and flew a United States flag. They killed between 150 and 200 people, mostly women, children and the elderly, and mutilated the bodies; a congressional commission condemned the massacre in 1865, but no one was prosecuted.

hechos/larga-caminata-navaja/titulo.texto: The Long Walk of the Navajos

hechos/larga-caminata-navaja/resumen.texto: After a scorched-earth campaign led by Kit Carson, which burned crops and killed livestock, some 8,000 to 9,000 Navajos were forced from 1864 to walk about 500 kilometers to the Bosque Redondo reservation in New Mexico, where a few hundred Mescalero Apaches had already been confined; hundreds died on the way and many more on the reservation, from hunger and disease. The 1868 treaty allowed them to return to part of their land.

hechos/confederacion-canadiense/resumen.texto: The British North America Act, passed by the British Parliament, on July 1, 1867 united the province of Canada, divided into Ontario and Quebec, with Nova Scotia and New Brunswick in the Dominion of Canada, with its capital at Ottawa. It gave the federal Parliament jurisdiction over “Indians, and Lands reserved for the Indians,” the basis of the Indian Act of 1876 and of the numbered treaties with the nations of the west.

hechos/ley-de-vacunacion-india-1832/titu.texto: The Law on Vaccinating Indigenous Peoples

hechos/ley-de-vacunacion-india-1832/resu.texto: In 1832 the United States Congress passed, and Andrew Jackson signed, a law that allocated federal funds to vaccinate Indigenous peoples against smallpox, one of the first federal health measures aimed at them. Its implementation was uneven: according to historian J. Diane Pearson (2003), Secretary of War Lewis Cass left out upper Missouri peoples such as the Mandans, Arikaras, Crees and Blackfeet, who were hit hard by the 1837 epidemic.

hechos/discurso-del-jefe-seattle/titulo.texto: Chief Seattle’s Speech and Its Versions

hechos/discurso-del-jefe-seattle/resumen.texto: Around 1854 or 1855 Si’ahl (Seattle), chief of the Suquamish and Duwamish, spoke before the governor of the Washington Territory, Isaac Stevens, but no text from that occasion survives. The first version was published in 1887 by physician Henry A. Smith, who said he reconstructed it from his notes, and the most widespread one, an environmentalist manifesto, was written around 1971 by screenwriter Ted Perry for a documentary; dozens of different versions have been gathered. What circulates as Chief Seattle’s “letter” or “speech” cannot be taken as his words.

lugares/san-agustin-florida/resumen.texto: Founded by Pedro Menéndez de Avilés in 1565 next to the Timucua village of Seloy, it was the capital of Spanish Florida and the base of its missions. It is the oldest city of European origin inhabited without interruption in the continental territory of the United States.

lugares/santa-fe-nuevo-mexico/resumen.texto: Villa founded around 1610 as the capital of New Mexico, besieged and taken by the Pueblo peoples in the 1680 revolt and recovered by Diego de Vargas in 1693. It is the oldest state capital in the United States.

lugares/quebec/resumen.texto: Founded by Champlain in 1608 on the site of the Iroquoian village of Stadacona, it was the capital of New France and the seat of its bishopric, seminary, hospital and Ursuline convent. It passed to Great Britain after the battle of 1759.

lugares/montreal/resumen.texto: Founded in 1642 as Ville-Marie, a mission of French devotees, on the island where Cartier had visited the Iroquoian village of Hochelaga in 1535. It was the center of New France’s fur trade and the site of the Great Peace of 1701.

lugares/jamestown/resumen.texto: The first permanent English settlement in America, founded in 1607 on land of the Powhatan Confederacy, and capital of Virginia until 1699. Excavations since 1994 found the original fort, which was thought to have been lost in the river.

lugares/filadelfia/resumen.texto: City founded by William Penn in 1682 on land bought from the Lenape. It was the largest city of the Thirteen Colonies and the seat of the Continental Congresses, of the Declaration of Independence and of the 1787 constitutional convention.

lugares/nueva-york/resumen.texto: Founded as New Amsterdam by the Dutch West India Company on the island of Manhattan, on Lenape territory, it was the capital of New Netherland until the English took it in 1664 and renamed it.

lugares/boston/resumen.texto: Founded in 1630 by the Puritans of the Massachusetts Bay Company on the Shawmut peninsula, it was the political and religious center of New England.

lugares/plymouth-massachusetts/resumen.texto: Founded in 1620 by the passengers of the Mayflower on the abandoned village of Patuxet, whose inhabitants had died in the 1616–1619 epidemic. It was the capital of the Plymouth Colony until 1691.

lugares/nueva-orleans/resumen.texto: Founded by Bienville in 1718 near the mouth of the Mississippi, it was the capital of French Louisiana and, from 1763 to 1800, of Spanish Louisiana. The United States bought it with Louisiana in 1803.

lugares/natick/resumen.texto: The first “praying town” of Christian Indians, founded by John Eliot in 1651 on the banks of the Charles River, with its own government and school. After King Philip’s War it lost population, and its lands gradually passed into the hands of colonists.

lugares/novoarkhangelsk/resumen.texto: Founded by Baranov in 1804 next to the Tlingit fort captured that year, it was the capital of Russian America until 1867; the transfer of Alaska to the United States took place there.

lugares/castillo-de-san-marcos/resumen.texto: Coquina stone fortress built between 1672 and 1695 to defend St. Augustine, partly with the labor of Indians from the missions. It withstood English sieges in 1702 and 1740.

lugares/fuerte-carolina/resumen.texto: Fort of the French Huguenots next to the San Juan River, in Timucua land, taken by Menéndez de Avilés in September 1565. Its exact location has not been found.

lugares/fuerte-mose/nombre.texto: Gracia Real de Santa Teresa de Mose

lugares/fuerte-mose/resumen.texto: Fortified town of Africans who had fled Carolina and gained their freedom in Spanish Florida, north of St. Augustine. Its inhabitants left for Cuba in 1763 when Florida passed to Great Britain.

lugares/mision-san-luis-de-apalache/resu.texto: Capital of the province of Apalachee, with a mission, a fort and the council house of the Apalachee chief, today reconstructed in Tallahassee on the basis of excavations. It was abandoned in 1704 in the face of attacks from Carolina.

lugares/palacio-de-los-gobernadores/nomb.texto: Palace of the Governors of Santa Fe

lugares/palacio-de-los-gobernadores/resu.texto: Seat of the government of New Mexico since around 1610, occupied by Pueblo peoples after the 1680 revolt and recovered in 1693. It is one of the oldest public buildings in the United States.

lugares/hawikuh/resumen.texto: Zuni pueblo where Estebanico died in 1539 and which Coronado took by assault in July 1540, believing it was Cíbola. It had a Franciscan mission from 1629 and was abandoned at the time of the 1680 revolt.

lugares/mision-de-san-antonio-de-valero/.texto: Mission San Antonio de Valero (The Alamo)
Franciscan mission founded in 1718 for Coahuiltecan peoples, origin of San Antonio. Secularized in 1793, its church became the Alamo fort in the Texas War of 1836.

lugares/mision-de-san-saba/nombre.texto: Mission Santa Cruz de San Sabá

lugares/mision-de-san-saba/resumen.texto: Mission for the Lipan Apaches in central Texas, destroyed in March 1758 by Comanches and Wichitas.

lugares/mision-san-diego/resumen.texto: First mission in Alta California, founded by Junípero Serra in July 1769 on Kumeyaay land. It was burned by the Kumeyaay in November 1775 and rebuilt.

lugares/mision-san-carlos/nombre.texto: Mission San Carlos Borromeo de Carmelo

lugares/mision-san-carlos/resumen.texto: Founded in Monterey in 1770 and moved to Carmel in 1771, it was the seat of the president of the California missions; Junípero Serra is buried there.

lugares/mision-san-gabriel/resumen.texto: Mission founded in 1771 on Tongva land, near present-day Los Angeles, and the scene of Toypurina’s attempted rebellion in 1785.

lugares/fort-ross/resumen.texto: Post of the Russian-American Company on the California coast, founded in 1812 on Kashaya Pomo land to supply wheat to Alaska and to hunt sea otters with Alutiiq hunters. It was sold in 1841.

lugares/bahia-de-tres-santos/resumen.texto: First permanent Russian settlement in America, founded by Shelikhov in 1784 on Kodiak Island; in 1792 the seat was moved to present-day Kodiak city.

lugares/fort-pitt/resumen.texto: British fort built at the confluence that forms the Ohio River, on the site of the French Fort Duquesne. It was besieged in 1763 during Pontiac’s Rebellion; it is the origin of Pittsburgh.

lugares/werowocomoco/resumen.texto: Capital of Powhatan on the York River, where John Smith was taken in 1607–1608. Identified and excavated since 2003, it shows occupation from around the 13th century and trenches that delimited a central enclosure.

lugares/sainte-marie-entre-los-hurones/r.texto: Fortified base of the Jesuit mission in Huronia, with a chapel, hospital and workshops, which the Jesuits burned in 1649 when they fled Iroquois attacks. It was rebuilt in the 20th century based on the excavations.

lugares/hotel-dieu-de-quebec/resumen.texto: Hospital founded in 1639 by the Augustinian Hospitallers of Dieppe with funds from the Duchess of Aiguillon; it first cared for Indigenous people and is the oldest hospital in operation in Canada.

lugares/monasterio-de-las-ursulinas-de-q.texto: Convent and girls’ school founded in 1639 by Marie de l’Incarnation, the first girls’ school in New France, which admitted French and Indigenous students.

lugares/seminario-de-quebec/resumen.texto: Seminary founded by Bishop Laval in 1663 to train the clergy of New France; Laval University was born from it in 1852.

lugares/universidad-de-harvard/resumen.texto: College founded by the Massachusetts assembly in 1636 to train ministers, the oldest institution of higher education in the United States. Its 1650 charter included the education of youth “English and Indian.”

lugares/colegio-de-william-and-mary/resu.texto: Royal college founded in Williamsburg, Virginia, in 1693, which from 1723 had a school for Indigenous children in the Brafferton building.

lugares/dartmouth-college/resumen.texto: College founded in Hanover, New Hampshire, by Eleazar Wheelock in 1769, with a charter that destined it for Indigenous and English youth, financed with what Samson Occom raised in Great Britain.
